#6747. Miley Cyrus Debuts Her Sculptural Wedding Band—Jewelers Explain the Design

Miley Cyrus did more than give fans a first look at her wedding dress when she shared photos of her nuptials on Sunday. Zoom in and the singer’s thick wedding band is visible, stacked with her gold bombé cushion-cut diamond engagement ring.

She later shared another look at her bridal jewelry, including her band, which appears to be in a black round ring box:

The singer’s band choice is fashion-forward, The Clear Cut’s founder Olivia Landau tells ELLE. “Thick wedding bands have been trending, whether they are larger diamond eternity bands or wider solid gold bands.”

It also really suits her, says Lauren Boc, founder and CEO of Hera Fine Jewelry: “Miley’s wedding set is a beautiful reflection of her personal style—it has some rock and roll edge but still feels upscale.”

Here, jewelers share their first impressions of the piece with ELLE.

Steph Mazuera, who founded her own namesake brand, says Cyrus’s ring has “a slightly curved silhouette” that “appears to follow the contours of her engagement ring.”

“When working with larger, bolder rings, introducing a soft curve or slight bend into the stack can make the overall combination feel more organic,” she adds. “It brings a sense of balance and softness without taking away from the impact of the individual rings. Everything should be designed to flow around the center stone.”

Based on the photos she shared, Cyrus’s engagement ring and wedding band appear to be different metals. Her engagement ring is yellow gold.

Her wedding band, meanwhile, “looks to be a half-round band, around 4 mm, in white gold or platinum,” Boc says. “It appears that there’s a small east-west oval diamond bezel-set on top of the band, similar to our Amir ring. Raising the diamond slightly above the band like this creates dimension.”

Several factors contribute to the value of a ring like Cyrus’s. “A custom band like this one could range quite a bit depending on the maker, gold weight, and craftsmanship,” Mazuera explains. “I would price a similar custom design in my studio in the $3,000–$5,000 range.”

Cyrus’s wedding band is a statement piece that can be worn with or without her engagement ring. “I like that her wedding band feels substantial enough to hold its own alongside her engagement ring without competing with it,” Mazuera says. “Both rings have a strong sculptural presence, but the slight curve of the wedding band helps the two sit together more naturally.”

Worn together, the two pieces have “a really bold look that’s both edgy and luxurious,” Boc says. “It’s maximalist, with a lot of metal on the hand. I love it!”

Cyrus’s wedding band is anything but minimalist—but that’s exactly why it fuels multiple jewelry trends.

“I think we’re seeing a continued move toward more sculptural, substantial wedding jewelry, moving away from the idea that wedding bands need to be delicate or understated,” Mazuera says.

Boc agrees. “Miley’s wedding set definitely reflects the trends we’re seeing at Hera. Chunky, bolder looks with a lot of gold weight have become really popular with our clients. When I first founded Hera in 2021, the big engagement ring trend was really thin, delicate-looking bands. As a jewelry designer who cares a lot about durability, I’m so happy to see people turning toward more substantial designs.”

Less traditional ring designs like Cyrus’s are also becoming more popular. “Our clients are often more concerned with having a ring that feels distinctive and uniquely like them,” Boc says.

Boc notes that while Cyrus’s photos give a limited view of her engagement ring and wedding band together, the apparent mix of metals is right on trend.

“I think there’s something so chic and effortless about a mixed metal stack,” she adds. “Like everything else about Miley’s stack, mixing metals is the kind of design decision that makes your wedding set really feel curated and chosen around a strong understanding of your personal style. She certainly didn’t just pick this up pre-designed at a big box store; a stack like this belongs to someone who’s confident in her personal style and chose something that feels uniquely her.”

#6745. “Two Girls Who Speak All the Time About Politics”: Tao Okamoto and Virginie Efira Take On Capitalism in All of a Sudden

Okamoto and Efira shared the Best Actress Award at Cannes, where All of a Sudden premiered this summer

We’re all seeking comfort as the world ends. Environmental, economic, and political pressures weigh heavily on our minds as tangible solutions feel farther and farther out of reach. Solace is a rare commodity in a world controlled by unrelenting capitalist forces. In All of a Sudden, filmmaker Ryusuke Hamaguchi suggests that as we face tragedy, we must remember our vital need for human connection.

All of a Sudden tells the story of two women who forge a formidable friendship as they face personal and professional hardship. Marie-Lou Fontaine (Virginie Efira) runs an elder-care facility near Paris, where she introduces a “Humanitude” methodology designed to treat patients with dignity and introduce listening-heavy caretaking practice. She befriends Mari (Tao Okamoto), a terminally ill theater director from Japan. Ryusuke chronicles this relationship through extended, emotional conversations, spoken in both Japanese and French, and covering topics from identity to mortality.

The film is an adaptation of a nonfiction book, When Life Suddenly Takes a Turn: Twenty Letters Between a Philosopher With Terminal Cancer and a Medical Anthropologist, which collects correspondence from two Japanese-speaking academics as they reflect on health care and death during the last few months of philosopher Makiko Miyano’s life (who inspired Okamoto’s character). Instead of keeping the fact that the two pen pals spoke the same language, he introduced French and moved the story to Paris. This small change forced the story to confront language gaps, exploring the power of conversation and listening and asserting that so much can be achieved through this mediation.

Efira and Okamoto understand their characters’ simmering anxieties and outlooks on the world, providing the bedrock for these impressively naturalistic performances. The two actresses sustain long, philosophical conversation with such intensity throughout the entire three hours and 16 minutes. In a rare occurrence, the two shared the Best Actress Award at the Cannes Film Festival, where the movie premiered this summer. In the film, their budding friendship serves as a sounding board for each other, as Marie-Lou grapples with the pressure of capitalism on her medical staff and Mari comes to terms with the end of her life. In typical fashion, Ryusuke lets the camera linger on these two actresses during these prolonged philosophical interactions, forcing the audience to sit with the gravity of their situations.

Ahead of the theatrical release of Ryusuke’s latest feature film, Bazaar spoke to Efira and Okamoto about the first time they read the script, how they built an intimate bond despite speaking two different languages, and the punk, anti-capitalist edge fueling this intimate, conversation-heavy film.

Tao Okamoto: It’s the scene where she talks about capitalism while writing on the whiteboard. That’s one of the strangest scenes in the movie. I felt connected to the character because I am also a climate activist myself. I’ve been spreading the word about climate crises on podcasts, and I talk about it daily. When I read the part, I felt, “I need to play this character.”

Virginie Efira: It’s the same for me, because this scene is so special. When I read it, the movie felt like one of the most profound, special, and radical readings. You have two girls who speak all the time about politics. We don’t see that. I never see that in other movies. Sometimes, when a director wants to put something philosophical, political, or intellectual, they say, “Maybe we’ll do three minutes,” otherwise the audience will be bored. No, this movie spent 15 minutes [discussing capitalism], and I said, “Oh yes, that’s so punk!” The film has its own language. When I read All of a Sudden, I could hear the language of the movie, and I wanted to approach it. When I met Tao, I thought, “Oh, we are so lucky to be an actress and work with [Ryusuke], but also to share this material with him.”

VE: I only knew one word in Japanese before making the movie. Then, to be able to speak Japanese at a high level, because the character studied in Japan, I must first learn to read, then learn to embody the language. Finding the language of the movie was strange. There’s a flat and natural way to play [in one of Ryusuke’s movies]. He spoke to me about Cassavetes and Gena Rowlands, but also about Bresson. Neutral performances. You find it when you open up, and when I opened to Tao, we discovered the right language for the movie. We did a lot of flat readings before shooting. We never rehearsed in motion, so when we finally performed for the first time, we awakened the text.

TO: I’m going to add that because I started my career in America, finding a middle ground by using a language that’s not my mother tongue is normal for me. On the surface, that part wasn’t a challenge for me. Finding the language for this film and respecting Hamaguchi’s way of working were priorities. We were naturally drawn to his talent and wanted to make his dream happen and be part of it.

TO: I joined this project way after Virginie. I luckily had months to prepare with him, and during rehearsals, you drop all emotion and read the text as if you were reading numbers. On top of that, I got to visit some institutes, such as the Cancer Research Center and places where people work with disabled people, to build up my understanding of my role’s point of view. Reading the text over and over was a unique experience for me. [Ryusuke] can really listen to the actor’s voice and tell the difference between someone who is simply reading and someone really concentrating. Even though you’re not supposed to put any emotions, you have to be present; you have to be there. I’ve never experienced such rich, profound preparation for a role.

VE: We shot in a real nursing home. There was a mix between fiction and reality. Sometimes filmmaking becomes standardized, with no room left to breathe, but with Hamaguchi, you’re sure he will leave room for the unexpected and for uncertainty. It allows you to embrace the unpredictability of reality. He’s not looking for an accident, but for the ability to be in the present. A viewer of Hamaguchi’s work will always feel a sensation of documentation, but it’s still always cinema. To be an actor in his movies is to be naturalistic, to be in the present, to capture some details and really embrace this unpredictability. The filming process becomes an adventure he wants you to have. One day, he told me, “I hope that you will find the light.” He said a lot of cryptic things. He said to me, “Don’t use your text like a tool; just go inside the text.”

TO: The script is already amazing. And I could read it over and over again, and that was a joy. But he mentioned that I should read the original book. It’s about two women exchanging letters—or emails. They are real people who the characters are modeled after. I wanted to please the people who know these women, not to make them too different from them. I first put pressure on myself to portray this woman as close to the real person, but it was impossible for me because this person passed away in 2019. I couldn’t do much research, so I interviewed her mother and the co-writer. That provided me with a lot of clues, but reading their exchanged letters already gave me the soul of this movie.

VE: He gives the book to the actresses, but also to the entire team. I never felt something so collective, and you will feel it in the movie, from the sound engineer to someone who only stayed two days on set. I also met the anthropologist. When you read this book, it’s full of life. It gives you a perceptible beauty of things. The book has a kind of energy; it helps you keep a level of optimism even when you know the situation is hopeless. In this book, it speaks about what it’s like to be alive. Maybe there’s beauty in life because we are going to die.

TO: For me, I came on this project at the last minute, only a month before. Virginie was so dedicated to studying Japanese from scratch; it was so impressive how she studied all this writing, reading, and lines. Seeing that, I had a huge admiration, like “Who can do this!?” As you can see, Virginie’s so charming; nobody would hate her. It was so easy for me to be drawn to her as a person, as the characters in the movie were discovering each other.

VE: We got to know each other through the shoot. I was happy not to know much at the beginning and to progressively get deeper into our relationship. We lived all that together. I conflate Marie-Lou’s feelings for Mari with Virginie’s feelings for Tao, because we share that. It will be an end, not a tragic one like in the movie, but it will be an end. But I know Tao will carry this experience in her heart forever, and I will too. He let us feel what we want to feel.

TO: I study environmental issues, and I always thought capitalism is responsible for our world’s issues. Something I didn’t know until I read this script was that capitalism doesn’t only exploit our environment, but also our human bodies—human labor and our time. When I connected those dots, I realized all the problems could be blamed on capitalism. We’re looking for time and looking for happiness—or security—and all these things can be related to a capitalistic way of living. I think it’s great that Hamaguchi connected that fundamental issue to Marie-Lou’s situation in the elderly home. She’s frustrated, as is Marie. She’s battling her cancer, and it can be connected to this economic issue.

VE: Cinema can show bodies, fatigue, and with Marie-Lou, you see a certain fatigue because capitalism creates it. How do we deal with that? We say, “Oh, capitalism’s not good. We don’t have time. And we want to be richer and richer.” But how do we fight that, because everything is already there? I come from France, and you see all the young people outside. The real question is, what can cinema do with that? It’s not a theoretical thing, but Hamaguchi can find a solution. It’s speaking, listening to the other, sharing ideas; it’s movement. If I look for a solution to this problem with money, I’ll remain a prisoner of this way of functioning. Even if you think you’re not in a stage of capitalism, you are.

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

#6744. 10 “Timeless” Design Choices Designers Say Will Always Be in Style

Step away from the trends and invest in these instead.

Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Pictured above: A refreshing sunroom with built-in bookshelves by Doniphan Moore.

While embracing home design trends can be fun for a while, it can get really old really quickly. Of course, if you really like something, then by all means, decorate your home with it. However, if you’re simply reaching for the things that are popular at a current moment in time before throwing them out after you realize you don’t actually like them, then it might be time to invest in some more timeless decor.

“Ultimately, timeless design is all about creating spaces that are beautiful, functional, and meaningful,” says Abby Pendergrast, an interior stylist and set designer. “That’s why people are drawn to these classics—they make a house feel like a home, and that never goes out of style.”

Ahead, we asked a handful of designers to share the pieces and choices they deem timeless. From gilded mirrors to striped textiles, keep reading to see the 10 things that designers promise you’ll love for years to come.

Antique chests and dressers will never go out of style because they’re well made piece that only get better with time.

“They were meant to last for many years, acting as heirloom pieces for generations to come,” says Debbie Mathews LeRoy of Debbie Mathews Antiques & Designs. They’re multifunctional to use as storage or a spare surface, and they can easily move from room to room and house to house.

“An antique chest brings history and warmth to any space,” designer Emily Jiles of Maggie Griffin Design explains. “Mixing in an antique chest gives the room a collected feel and adds character that new furniture often can't replicate.”

Golden mirrors add a touch of elegance to any room, and they’re shockingly versatile. They can bring more luxury to a traditional style home, or they can add a historic air to a more modern space. Mathews LeRoy, however, specifically adores Louis Philippe giltwood mirrors.

“It can live happily in a traditional interior or fit within a transitional interior thanks to its simple arched shape with minimal decoration,” she says. “They boast understated elegance and can be beautiful in an entrance hall or foyer, dining room, living room, powder room, or bedroom!”

Like any classic choice, bookshelves will grow with you as your sensibility evolves and changes. They can be endlessly re-styled and adjusted to hold whatever pieces you acquire along the way. Plus, they are a kind of diary of the books you are reading and the conversations you are having.

“Literature never goes out of style. A home without books isn’t a home in my opinion. And a bookshelf acts as a blank canvas to explore your innate curatorial abilities,” says Alex Bass, founder and CEO of Art Advisory & Interior Design Studio Salon 21. “It is also something that grows with you and that you can constantly reorganize. So investing in a good one with timeless appeal is key.”

High-quality natural materials such as wood or stone just get better with time. “Using natural materials in your home is always a good idea,” says Pendergrast. “They bring warmth, texture, and that feeling of authenticity we all crave.”

Wood, whether it’s flooring, furniture, or even ceiling beams, adds a cozy, lived-in vibe, while stone is durable and elegant. “Wood and stone age gracefully, developing character as the years go by. They’re versatile enough to fit into any style, from modern to rustic, which means you won’t have to worry about them ever going out of fashion,” she says.

While we're on the topic of natural materials, let's not forget this inimitable combination. Marble and wood both have a knack for adding character and aging beautifully, and they're not just for kitchens. Think: Wooden chairs pulled up to a marble-topped dining table or a wood coffee table or console with a marble top. The combination is “both timeless, modern, and neutral while bringing a luxurious feel to your space,” says Bass.

Leather furniture carries memories—as a piece ages, its patina changes. And a leather chair can hold its own—the material has weight and personality that make it an excellent companion to a wide range of nearby colors, fabrics, and patterns. “It fits any type of design aesthetic, whether you’re going for something more mid-century or more traditional,” Bass says. “I love seeing the wear in a piece, the cracks and the wrinkles.”

Sticking with paint colors inspired by nature—such as soft blues, calming greens, whites, and warm tans—helps create a peaceful and balanced space. “These colors are easy on the eyes and make your home feel more like a retreat,” Pendergrast says. “Earthy, natural shades are always in style because they have this effortless way of grounding a space. They act like neutrals, so you can easily switch up your decor over the years without having to repaint the whole place.”

A wooden table, such as an antique farm table, is a timeless piece worth investing in. As demonstrated in this space designed by Clara Jung of Banner Day Interiors, it grounds the room, allowing other decor choices to be light and airy. Whether it’s a coffee table, side table, or made for a dining room, “You’ll always find use for it and it’s something sturdy that will never go out of style,” Bass says.

Stripes are a classic pattern that doesn’t ever feel too trendy. “You can throw them on curtains, rugs, or even wallpaper, and they’ll add a bit of structure without overpowering the room,” Pendergrast says. “Whether you go bold or keep it subtle, stripes always find a way to fit in.” The best part about stripes is how flexible they are. “They work with just about any style, and because they’re so simple, they won’t clash with other patterns or elements in your space,” she adds.

Built-in details such as crown molding or wainscoting give your space instant character. Your home may already have these features, but if it doesn’t, they are often simple additions you can implement. “These features add a little polish without feeling too stuffy, and they make the room feel more custom and unique,” Pendergrast says. “Crown molding and wainscoting have been around for ages, and they’re not going anywhere.” These architectural details are subtle ways to add depth and elegance to a room. Even better is that they can blend with any style, whether your vibe is traditional or modern.

#6741. Omega and Swatch Just Launched a New MoonSwatch—and No Two Are the Same

The Mission to Earthphase – Silver Snowflake, the 39th watch in the series, will have collectors keeping an eye on the Swiss weather forecast.

By MoonSwatch standards, it’s been a quiet year. Swatch has been otherwise occupied with the Audemars Piguet Royal Pop, the May release for which people lined up for six days in New York, police deployed tear gas in France, and which, according to Swatch Group, has generated more than 25 billion views on social media.

Not that interest in the MoonSwatch has gone away.

An estimated 4.5 million have been sold since the collaboration began in March 2022 (and that figure only takes us to the end of 2024). In July this year, some 1.2 million people applied to buy one of the 1,969 examples of its $570 Mission to the Moon 1969, a watch that incorporated 11 grams of 18-carat gold recycled from vintage Omega components.

The latest MoonSwatch—only the third new model this year, compared with 11 in 2023—is the Mission to Earthphase – Silver Snowflake.

An all-black counterpart to last winter’s all-white Cold Moon edition, it takes as its starting point the idea that no two snowflakes are alike.

Swatch has developed a digital process capable of generating millions of different snowflake patterns, one of which is laser-engraved onto the moonphase indicator of each watch. So, unusually for a mass-produced quartz watch, every example is unique.

It also features the complication Swatch introduced in November 2024 and which remains exclusive to the MoonSwatch: an earthphase indicator. Where a conventional moonphase shows the phases of the Moon as viewed from Earth, this does the reverse. The two displays run in opposite directions over the same 29.5-day cycle.

(How useful this is to those of us who live on Earth is debatable, but it’s one of the more original ideas in watchmaking in recent years.)

There are some nice details elsewhere on the 42mm Bioceramic watch, including Snoopy and Woodstock in the snow, a pair of miniature skis at 11 o’clock, and a tiny patch of white on the Earth representing a snow-covered Switzerland, which glows green under UV light.

As with last year’s winter edition, there’s a stipulation.

The watch goes on sale at selected Swatch stores worldwide on Black Friday, November 27. After that, until March 20, 2027, the last day of winter, you’ll only be able to buy one when it’s snowing in Switzerland.

Swatch will be providing weather updates on its website.

Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Pictured above: A living room area designed by Kristen Thomas of Ink & Canvas Design

A fresh coat of paint is one of the easiest ways to give your home a little refresh before the holidays, but you don't necessarily have to take on an entire redesign project to make an impact.

Some of the most interesting places to introduce color are the details you might normally overlook. They're relatively small surfaces, but a little paint can make them feel like intentional design features, adding character and definition without the time, expense, or commitment of repainting every wall.

Whether you want to make a statement, add a little contrast, or create a more interesting backdrop, there are plenty of ways to make a big visual impact with a relatively small project. Ahead, designers share the unexpected spots worth painting before the holidays and how to choose colors that feel right at home.

Window casings are an easy detail to overlook, especially when they're painted the same white as the walls and trim throughout the house. But introducing a little color around the windows “can emphasize the proportions of a window and give the room more definition,” says designer Sarah Cole. Even if you're not ready to go bold, she adds that “a subtle contrast can make a difference.”

For a more traditional look, Kristen Thomas of Ink & Canvas Design recommends pulling from a historical or traditional palette, pointing out that “colored trim was once a sign of status in early American homes” because rich pigments were costly and difficult to come by.

When time is tight before the holidays, this simple painting project can be achieved in a single afternoon. Just don’t forget the painter’s tape.

Don't overlook the design impact of the interior doors in your home—a hallway lined with plain white doors can feel a little forgettable, but painting one or two in a contrasting shade can give the space a more intentional look. Paint it early enough, and you may be able to hang a wreath from it.

Massimo Buster Minale, founder and creative director of Buster + Punch, believes an accent like this “can completely shift the character of a room.” And you don't necessarily need to choose a bright or dramatic color to get that effect. Picking one you love, rather than going all-in on a trendy shade, is key.

“I recommend choosing a grounding color and adding some whimsy with the small touches,” says Lee Crowder, National Director of Design and Model Experience at Taylor Morrison. Before painting, take a look at the doors in adjoining rooms so you can decide whether a single standout door or a more consistent color story makes the most sense.

If you have built-in bookshelves or cabinetry, you already have a natural spot for a little color. Rather than repainting the entire unit, try painting just the back panels. This also gives you the opportunity to declutter what’s already there. Cole recommends this pre-holiday spot because “it adds depth and helps books and collections stand out.” Her advice for choosing a shade? “Pull a color from the room's upholstery, rug or artwork.”

Thomas also recommends painting built-in shelving and cabinetry as a way to create a special feature in the room. “Painting built-ins sets them apart as a special feature and creates a beautiful backdrop for your favorite objects and holiday decor,” she says.

Instead of going for a bold contrasting hue, Vivian Robins at Arketa Design Studio suggests using a color that already appears elsewhere in the space, explaining that this small paint update can work as a “punctuation mark” in the room.

“Sometimes the smallest design changes create the biggest impression within a room because you're drawing out a color that lives in the space,” Robins adds.

#6733. Couples Need to Stop Being So Weird About GTA 6

Grand Theft Auto VI came out last Thursday, and somehow the most unbearable thing about it isn't the grown men playing the game—it's the couples.

After the release of the game, my feed became a nonstop slideshow of printed contracts, handmade gift baskets, and girlfriends narrating their boyfriends' disappearance into Vice City like it's a deployment. Couples posted printed agreements that grant the player 10 full days of uninterrupted access.

I'm not here to tell anyone not to play a video game. People should do what makes them happy. But why are we all being so weird about a video game?

Ten days off from the relationship, so a man can play a game. I'd like to meet the woman who has ever been granted a 10-day leave from her partner, her family, her job, and the emotional labor of every relationship in her life. Women don't get to just disappear to pursue their hobbies.

Some women in relationships are putting together “offerings” for their partner. One viral example involved a GTA-themed gift basket stocked with snacks and drinks for the player's sessions. Another woman posted a Target-run basket of her boyfriend's favorite snacks with the caption, "This is your sign to make your man a GTA 6 basket!"

No. It's not. When was the last time he made you a basket for one of your hobbies?

On the flip side, some men are gifting their partners a basket, with the idea that women need something in return—a little distraction to keep busy while he's busy. Women are not toddlers who need to be handed a snack and a coloring book while the grown-ups play. We have friends. We have jobs. We have entire lives that existed before his Rockstar account and will exist after it. We'll be fine. We might even enjoy the quiet!

It all begs the question: Why can't men just have hobbies like normal people? Women have hobbies all the time. We go to pilates, we read, we get absorbed in a show, and nobody drafts a legal document. Let’s keep up that energy. Just play the game and also make time for the rest of your life!

But it isn’t just about people finding the time to play the game. There’s separate discourse among couples about the relationship players maintain with Lucia, the main female character.

Online, some women have expressed feeling jealous of Lucia. Around the game's lead-up, users on TikTok and Instagram were claiming that boyfriends who nurture a virtual relationship with Lucia could be considered cheating. A YouGov poll of 4,000 adults found around 6 percent would consider dating in games like GTA VI to be infidelity. That's a generally small number, but it's still making headway on social media.

Lucia is a character. She is pixels. If your relationship can be undone by a woman who exists only to rob a gas station with your boyfriend, the problem was never Lucia.

To be fair, some women have leaned into the joke. One girlfriend gifted her boyfriend the game with a four-rule counter-contract that ended with the line "Lucia is not your real girlfriend." I respect the bit—but it still icks me out.

On the other hand, there have been people claiming that GTA 6 is teaching men to be better partners. I’d like to politely disagree. The theory goes that watching Jason treat Lucia well, and putting effort into that relationship on screen, will make players better boyfriends in real life.

I'm glad they're being attentive to Lucia. I mean that. It’s a nice change to see the video game encouraging men to be decent human beings (though the bar is low). But at the end of the day, they're buying flowers, fixing things up, and doing the emotional work for a woman who doesn't exist, while their actual girlfriends are across the room eating a basket of Swedish Fish.

Can we all get real for a second? What grown man needs a video game to teach him how to treat a partner? Showing up, communicating, and putting in effort are not secret skills only unlocked by a video game. I promise you your boyfriend is not learning valuable relationship skills playing GTA 6.

So to any couples out there being particularly weird about GTA 6: play the game, enjoy it, and please just be normal. Be a person with a hobby. It really isn't that deep.

#6731. 7 Home Organizing Trends That Will Be EVERYWHERE in 2027, According to Pros

Your clutter-free future starts with what you already own.

Although trends prevail in the interior design world, they also can find their way into other areas beyond decor—such as home organization. Creating orderly spaces can make life a lot easier. While tried-and-true solutions are still around, there are always fresh ways to tackle organizing projects.

As we look to the year ahead, four professional organizers are here to share what they think will be the top organizing trends.

While AI has been all over the place, from work to our personal lives—it appears to be tapering off, according to Lenora O’Keith, decluttering and organizing expert and owner of Aronel Home.

“AI and smart home solutions were everywhere at the beginning of the year, but there’s definitely been a lot of AI fatigue and a push for ‘dumb tech’ lately,” she shares. “When working with clients, a lot of them are over AI being added into everything. They just want simple solutions that work.” This can include things like setting up a household command center and labeling storage containers.

Moving has traditionally been a stressful experience that you were expected to figure out on your own—but that may be changing. Allison Flinn, owner of Reclaim Professional Organizing, says that more people are taking advantage of organizing services when they move.

“You can pack and unpack, but you won't truly have a fully functional and an organized new home if you haven't decluttered prior to moving or aren't intentional during the unpacking process by implementing a system that truly works for your lifestyle,” she says.

Instead of doing what a lot of us do—devising storage systems for each individual space—2027 may welcome the idea that you should treat your home as an entire unit to be organized.

Michelle Urban, owner and founder of The Organized House, says that people are increasingly not treating each room as its own one-off organizing project. She says that instead, they’re looking at how belongings move from one space to another and where they need to be throughout the day. For instance, items like backpacks, shoes, and sports gear may land in the entry, get stored in the garage, and need to be back by the door the next morning.

“When those spaces are planned together, the system supports the family’s routine instead of just moving things from one pile to another,” Urban says.

Viewed more holistically, experts are also seeing that organizing isn’t just an occasional task, but something to stay on top of each week. “I think more homeowners will begin to view organization as ongoing home maintenance rather than a one-time project,” says Ashley Bailey, founder and professional organizer at Everything Orderly. “Just like other aspects of maintaining a home, organizing requires occasional attention as our lives and needs change.”

Flinn says that more and more people are outsourcing household tasks to a home manager or home concierge. In addition to handling things like doing laundry, returning packages, and making doctor’s appointments, these professionals can also help you organize your home in just a few hours a week.

Eco-friendly everything is still as popular as ever, and it even applies to how we organize our homes. While O’Keith says that sustainability never really goes out of style, homeowners are increasingly turning to eco-friendly organizing products—specifically, by avoiding plastic and embracing natural materials like bamboo, rattan, and sea grass for baskets and bins.

But she says that there is a exception for basements and attics. “I always recommend heavy-duty plastic storage [for these areas],” O’Keith says. “Since those spaces deal with dampness, temperature changes, and pests, other materials could get damaged easily.”

While it can be lovely to live in a well-designed, beautiful home, if there isn’t function, you might make your daily life more difficult. That’s why people are going beyond Instagram-ready interiors and are wrapping in plenty of function.

Urban believes that progressively more people are bringing functional storage into a room’s design, and it isn’t just an add-on.

“A credenza can hold games in the living room; a dining room buffet can store wrapping paper and party decor between celebrations,” Urban points out. “As rooms take on more jobs, people want storage that looks like it belongs and does a useful job.”

As we head into 2027, people are thinking about their budgets more and more, which is why using items you already have as storage solutions is cost-effective.

“I'm seeing more clients interested in making better use of what they already own rather than automatically purchasing new organizing products,” Bailey says. For instance, she recently took on a project that transformed a playroom, but used items the family already had.

“Sometimes the best solution isn't another organizing product. It's rethinking how you're using the space and what you already have,” she says. “I think we'll see more emphasis on thoughtful editing and repurposing before purchasing something new.”

#6728. Why Do We All Love a Small-Town Holiday Romance? Guarding Stars Might Have the Answer

The fantasy of falling in love in a small town has surprisingly little to do with the small town itself.

I’ll find any excuse to cozy up with a holiday rom-com, so when Guarding Stars dropped on Netflix, it was a no-brainer. Gossip Girl and Supernatural alumni Leighton Meester and Jared Padalecki are embracing one of my favorite tropes: the good old “small-town holiday romance.” Leighton’s character Hannah goes with Jared’s character Jack to his hometown pretending to be his girlfriend, while actually serving as his bodyguard. It got me thinking: Whether we’re die-hard city dwellers or seasoned travelers, why do we still love the home-for-the-holidays romance trope?

For me, the answer lies in how this specific genre taps into our own deep-rooted desire for escapism. We’ve seen these kinds of fake girlfriend or friends-to-lovers storylines play out a million times before, so their predictability is incredibly comforting to watch. We have, quite literally, seen this film before. And during the heightened chaos of the holiday season, it places viewers in the safe bubble many people crave.

Plus, the small-town setting in Guarding Stars is perfectly cozy. The two head to Jack’s obnoxiously large family home in Montana that’s been pristinely decorated in Nancy Meyers–inspired aesthetics. And much like in one of my favorite holiday movies, The Family Stone, the house itself is just part of the fantasy. The idea of being welcomed into a close-knit community with acceptance might be exactly what we dream of the holidays being like. Being loved by a family that, in the case of Hannah, is not even your own is really intoxicating.

Even the dating looks more fun. Hannah and Jack spend the whole movie dating their way around town, doing cutesy romantic things like attending the local rodeo, getting caught on a kiss cam, and mucking out horses together in the family stables. These wouldn’t be your go-to date locations in a more urban, city-based setting, so their dating experience feels playful and different from everyday life.

And Guarding Stars finds a way to elevate this trope. Hannah isn’t actively looking for a man when all of this unfolds. She’s just doing her job as a bodyguard when she inadvertently falls into a snowball of festive shenanigans. Hannah is doing fine on her own, but there’s something sweet about watching her let her guard down. Guarding Stars gently suggests that by Hannah making herself a little more vulnerable, she’s making room for more people to love and support her. As someone who tends to handle the hard stuff alone (eldest daughter syndrome, anyone?), that really resonated with me.

So often, this genre leans toward women going to the small town and being “fixed” or changed by the relationship they encounter. Their lives in the big city are unsatisfying, actually, and they really would rather work at the Christmas tree farm. That doesn’t happen here. She ends up back in New York City, and that’s where the final action set piece of the movie happens.

Guarding Stars shows that the small-town holiday romance trope can change and evolve without losing its festive magic, because it’s about comfort and connection. We can be cozy and keep our apartments in New York City, and I’m thankful for that this holiday season.

#6727. All Aboard Fashion’s Absurd Hat Train

Swim caps and train conductor hats: The runway’s most theatrical headwear is made for standing out.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Fashion can’t get enough of freaky hats lately. Following the main character hat trend from a few seasons past, this time headwear has gone totally theatrical and over-the-top. Between Chanel’s fin-embellished Nemo-esque swim caps and Junya Watanabe’s super camp, oversize ’70s baker-boy-style caps, headpieces are seemingly obsessed with transforming their wearers into outlandish personas. And at a time when clothing is centered on escapism and storytelling, an eccentric chapeau might just be the most perfect finishing touch.

Simone Rocha’s sequin-embellished bonnets with chin straps might turn you into a living doll. Celebs, too, have already gotten the memo: Elle Fanning recently wore a Stephen Jones-designed makeup compact headpiece to match her Givenchy dress inspired by an archival piece he created over three decades ago, while doing press for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. Elsewhere, Cardi B showed up in a white embellished gown from Tamara Ralph’s spring 2026 couture collection, styled with a huge, showgirl-style feather hat. Ciara walked the Junya Watanabe spring/summer 2027 runway while wearing a bedazzled helmet dripping with chains.

At Vaquera’s spring/summer 2027 show titled “I’m a put-on-a-show kind of girl,” the neon high-octane gowns were counterbalanced with huge, satirical boater hats, followed by a weird and whimsical chef hat and maid headpiece paired with shrunken, mini bloomer uniform onesies. Adding more humor to the collection, the designers ended the show by performing a live karaoke version of Sonny & Cher’s “I Got You Babe.” The brand is the king of the theatrical character hat. For fall/winter 2026, it showcased pillbox-style hats that eclipsed the face with cutouts for the eyes, fencing-mask-inspired headwear, and an elongated train conductor hat that resembles a cross between The Rockettes Toy Soldier costumes and English bearskin caps.

Transforming is exactly the point: “Vaquera has always celebrated fashion’s transformative power,” read Vaquera’s show notes. “The collection confronts the tension between perfection and chaos. Can you be unhinged and complete at once? Its cast of characters—distorted drab mods, twisted ladies who lunch, abstracted leather daddies—all seem to suggest that the most covetable clothes for your future are those that mirror our fractured present.”

While years of the past were defined by singular aesthetics, 2026 lacks one solo homogeneous style. Formality, too, has been traded for casual looks. Hats used to be ubiquitous; now they’re sort of a rare dying breed, save for a baseball cap.

Perhaps that’s one of the reasons why these character-driven hats are so prevalent now. Many of them are tied to uniforms, occupations, or the everyday made extreme. It’s beautiful absurdism, verging on delightfully unhinged. Consider an over-the-top hat pure whimsy.

The best winter gloves keep your hands warm without making your fingers useless—and look good while they’re at it. We’ve rounded up our favorites, from waterproof, windproof pairs built for rough weather to stylish options that still keep your hands nice and toasty. And yes, plenty have touchscreen-compatible fingertips so you can still call and text (and play the Wordle). See our favorite pairs below.

These luxurious leather gloves come from Overland, the brand behind some of our favorite coats. Having a warm pair of gloves that actually does its job well is even more important for my boyfriend, who has Raynaud’s and needs extra protection for his hands, and the gloves he relies on year after year? #6719. Of Course Trump Found a Way to Plug His Big, Ugly Ballroom When Partaking in a Beloved Thanksgiving Tradition

The idea of turkeys in that Gilded Palace of Sin is just too damn on the nose.

(Alternative Musical Accompaniment to the Last Post of the Week from the Blog’s Favourite Living Canadian)

We’re battening down here for the predicted Thanksgiving Gale. (The famous Perfect Storm is known as the Halloween Gale. We name storms like that. We are fcking adorable that way.) Apparently, this mother is going to slam the entire northeast corridor from Washington to Maine. Which means massive chaos at a number of very busy airports. And given the performance of the secretary of transportation and the secretary of homeland security when a squirrel recently got into the wiring in El Dorado, Arkansas, I have never been more glad not to be traveling this weekend. At least we will be spared another goony-bird press conference from Sean Duffy and Markwayne Mullin, referred to by writer and musician David Ferguson immortally as Dumb and Plumber. That’s a keeper.

It’s going to be tough to fly, tougher to take a train, and even tougher than that to drive. And the storm is going to lock people indoors with their obnoxious relatives, which can only lead to alcoholic embarrassments and domestic mayhem. Of course, it always could be worse. We’re all being stuck in the house by the elements of the natural world, whereas the folks in Iowa and all over the Midwest are being gifted with a cornucopia of toxic clouds for the holiday. From The New York Times:

What’s worse? Being stuck in the house with Meemaw, who found the bourbon, or being stuck in the family van, heading south, with Meemaw, who found the bourbon? The Army’s got your back, Iowa, but pack a bag and scout out a route to Honduras anyway. Wow.

And I’m sure this last-minute FEMA warning didn’t confuse anyone.

Don’t just do something, dammit, stand there.

And not for nothing, but the Army’s been acting sketchy about this whole business almost from jump. From The Washington Post:

Did the president use the charming tradition of pardoning a turkey for Thanksgiving as an excuse for plugging his Gilded Palace of Sin? (Thanks, Gram.) What do you think? From Axios:

Turkeys in that ballroom are just too damn on the nose.

The 2026 midterm elections continue to bless us. Representative Scott DesJarlais, perhaps the worst human ever elected to the House of Representatives, is gone baby gone, beaten by Democratic candidate Victoria Broderick. DesJarlais’s rap sheet is nigh unprecedented. This all came out in 2012, and the voters kept sending this guy back to Washington by fat margins until two weeks ago. He lost to Broderick, a proudly pansexual 34-year-old mother of two whom he beat handily in 2024. However, since then, the Republican Tennessee legislature brilliantly redrew the maps, adding slices of Nashville to the Fourth Congressional District, a change that benefitted Broderick. So not only is Congress liberated from the likes of DesJarlais, but Broderick’s win was also another example of how Republican ratfcking of the redistricting process bit them on the ass. Heh, heh, heh.

Weekly WWOZ Pick to Click: “Happy Days” (McCoy Tyner): Yeah, I pretty much still love New Orleans.

Weekly Visit to the Pathé Archives: Here, from 1940, is FDR celebrating Thanksgiving with the patients at the Warm Springs polio facility where he once was a patient. The narrator makes a funny about the U.S. joining “the war” against polio. FDR chats up a young patient who is chowing down on a turkey leg that is as big as her head. It looks like it was fun to have a real president.

Discovery Corner: Hey, look what we found! From Live Science:

I have to say, a “floating castle” sounds like a terrible idea, and wearing chain mail on a floating castle sounds like an even worse one. If the floating castle blows up and sinks, then it’s fairly hard to swim in chain mail.

Old King Hans has come down as a jolly old soul, but he was quite the political schemer. He also died in one of those prosaic ways kings died in those days. He fell from his horse.

Hey, SciNews, is it a good day for dinosaur news? It’s always a good day for dinosaur news!

Once again, I point out that paleontology doesn’t necessarily require sweating over some limestone cliff face. Grab a sandwich and a soda and hit the drawers of the file cabinets in museum basements. Surprises like this make me happy they lived then.

In honor of the holiday, I will not close with the usual recitation of the nation’s woes. But do spare a thought for the people—and the cows, and the sheep—under the plume in the Midwest. Make sure, however, to be grateful for all those things that warm your heart and make all your lights shine. And all say amen.

#6701. What Is GTA VI Trying to Say About the Manosphere?

What’s a man allowed to like these days? Not the Super Bowl, or Christopher Nolan movies, it seems, each of them guilty of sins against masculinity. Now there is a new offender: Grand Theft Auto VI. Over one brief weekend, Rockstar’s long-in-the-works, exorbitantly expensive opus has given us a rare monocultural moment and elicited a wounded reaction from a slice of gamers steeped in the streams and podcasts of right-wing figures like Steven Crowder, Zack “Asmongold” Hoyt, and Braden Eric “Clavicular” Peters.

We asked a physical therapist, developers, and other gaming obsessives for the best tips to help you highjack garbage trucks in Leonida for as long as humanly possible.

Grand Theft Auto VI, these men assert, is emasculating because it asks players to role-play a man that respects his partner and do mundane tasks she would appreciate, like repaint their bedroom or get her a nice necklace. For others, it is less that the game is offensively woke and more that its wokeness is getting in the way of their fun. “You can’t kiss anyone other than your strong female Latina partner,” complains Crowder, his cohosts all lamenting that video games ought to be a vehicle for their every base fantasy. These men object to what they see as politics encroaching on what they think ought to be a politics-free space, “shut up and dribble” but for violent video games. But there’s a delicious irony to this because the game genuinely has a bone to pick with these unfortunate figureheads of the manosphere.

The manosphere, it should be noted, is a (shitty) state of mind. Less a formal designation than a collection of people who promote similar sexist, racist, and/or fascist ideals, a loose web of podcasters, streamers, and influencers who all preach a gospel of grievance in which men are victims of women withholding sex, liberals withholding power, and other men for not performing masculinity correctly. They can run the gamut from disgraced influencer Andrew Tate (currently in jail awaiting trial for a litany of alleged crimes) to the comedians and podcasters orbiting Joe Rogan’s massive audience. But they all have one thing in common: These men and the people who pay rapt attention to them are the targets of Grand Theft Auto VI’s satire.

Some background here: While yes, Grand Theft Auto VI casts players as modern Bonnie and Clyde Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, their story is only one reason to play the game. Another is the incredibly dense setting of Leonida, a feverish and astonishingly lifelike take on Florida, chock-full of weirdos and wildlife to take in. Layered on top of that is a whole media ecosystem: a fake Instagram to scroll named Snapmatic, a news feed app, a suite of radio stations with robust programming including two talk radio stations, three TV networks with entire shows, and magazines and books you can read in excerpts.

It’s in all this background material that Grand Theft Auto VI really tears into the modern grievance grift of the manosphere. The game’s decade-plus gestation means it’s had a lot of time to amass a shooting gallery of noxious conservative male influencers that the algorithm has elevated and buried, ranging from flat-earth conspiracy theorists to MAHA-adjacent cronies. On the Weazel TV network, you can find these views as the punchline of entire Adult Swim–esque cartoons like Right Wing, about a patriotic superhero horrified to learn that a straight pride parade has been transformed by a gay superhero called the Flamer. “All these years suppressing who I was, but now I’m free!” shouts Right Wing’s colleague Great Uncle Sam after the Flamer has liberated him. “Isn’t that what America is all about?” “No,” Right Wing retorts. “America is about guns, and lots of them!”

Scroll through Snapmatic, and you can find a clear analogue of Liver King—the content creator who promoted an “ancestral lifestyle” that involved consuming raw animal organs—posting under @paleoprimal. In one of his faux influencer videos, he advises his followers to “start beating your meat,” before dropkicking a hunk of raw flesh. “I don’t eat anything unless I’ve conquered it first.” Ashes of Glory, a sendup of historical war fiction that sits by Jason’s bed, is drowning in overly reverent prose that also happens to note that its war heroes are psychopaths. One passage: “'You’ve been charged with murdering civilians, violating every law known to God and man, calling your enemies rude names, and uncontrollable teabagging,’ said the General. 'Which is exactly why we need your help.’”

A lot of these blows are glancing, more about attacking attitudes than people, give or take a Liver King. But turn the in-game radio dial to WKTT, Grand Theft Auto VI’s conservative talk radio station, and the targets sharpen. Hosts Richard Bastion (Jason Sudeikis) and Dominic “The Brick” Brizzolato (Stavros Halkias) do pastiches of Alex Jones and Nick Fuentes, spouting racist and sexist takes. Ponytails are “the hairstyle of someone who’s about to suck your dick,” per Brizzolato, who also maintains local football team the Manatees have problems to do with “culture” and “not race.” Every so often they are undercut by callers who ask how performance-enhancing drugs and hair implants don’t count as gender-affirming care. Of the many items they hawk—Flaming O’s snacks, Sprunk soda, and Patriot beer—the most absurd and on-the-nose is a special playing card set with “no queens.”

In its blunt re-creation of the conservative male media ecosystem, Grand Theft Auto VI plainly states what Rockstar thinks of these guys: They’re really fucking stupid. They are stupid in ways that are true to life and moronic in ways that Rockstar exaggerates, but only just so. They drive home this point by underlining the pathetic loneliness subtextual in all these real-life broadcasts, with Richard Bastion asserting that he doesn’t have friends but is building “a fraternity with a mission to save America” and that friends “let you down” and “tell the papers that your wife sleeps in a separate bed and sometimes house.”

After 13 years, and a budget rumored to rival that of Dubai’s Burj Khalifa skyscraper, the new Grand Theft Auto is finally here. Our critic's verdict? It's a tour de force that reimagines what a video game can be.

The message hits cleaner than past iterations of the game not because Grand Theft Auto VI is any less lowbrow than before—it is still awash in dick jokes, memes about shitting your pants, and South Park–esque lambasting of White America—but because this more richly detailed, lifelike version of Grand Theft Auto means the cartoonish aspects stand out all the more. What’s a joke and what is not is clearer than it has ever been.

Despite the protests from fans who say the latest iteration of Grand Theft Auto betrays the spirit of the franchise, there was always evidence that the game hated these hypermasculinity-obsessed tryhards, even before they had a manosphere to inhabit. While early games in the series did not have much in the way of plot or characters, they were tongue-in-cheek caricatures of gangster epics and the ambitions of men within them, a touch of arch Scottish humor (Rockstar’s lead Grand Theft Auto team is based in Edinburgh) keeping them from being sincere homages.

Nearly 20 years ago in Grand Theft Auto IV—a series turning point, where the games started to have stories with intentional thematic interests—Rockstar Games incessantly lambasted the pursuit of the hypermasculine. Its protagonist Niko Bellic served as a stoic counterpoint to many of the jacked-up weirdos of the faux New York dubbed Liberty City, arriving in the United States during the game’s opening credits with nothing but the clothes on his back and his cousin Roman’s lies about his own success in his ear. Through Niko’s journey, Grand Theft Auto IV posed the arguments that this country’s obsession with the unfettered pursuit of power and wealth makes people unwell and that culture afflicts men in ways that render them uniquely delusional. It gives his cousin Roman a fantasy of a success that will never come, causing him to submit to the intimidations of two-bit enforcers. It makes men like Brucie Kibbutz, a supplement-obsessed fitness freak, deny his own obvious interest in men in favor of a nonstop stream of homophobic jokes and crude sexual banter. It makes Niko, a soldier who thought he was escaping his criminal past, find himself immediately becoming a different kind of criminal at the behest of men who believe the world is theirs to take. And that’s just in the first few hours.

Grand Theft Auto IV’s skewering came at the expense of others—namely the women and queer people who are the butt of nearly every joke in the game. Seven years later, Grand Theft Auto V would course-correct by being hateful to everyone in its fictional version of Los Angeles: the acai-and-granola liberals and the asshole conservatives alike. It mires itself in the desperation of male entitlement, as three characters—the middle-aged Michael De Santa, the young striver Franklin Clinton, and Trevor Philips, the lewd loose cannon—adjust poorly to a world they cannot dominate. De Santa, arguably the protagonist of the three characters the player can inhabit, sees the world as out to emasculate him, either through his wife’s affair, his deadbeat son, or his daughter, who he must rescue from TV producers that he assumes are predatory. Michael’s world is much simpler when he’s holding a gun, and Grand Theft Auto V is eager to get one in his hands. In this, it feels like the game wants you to agree: Isn’t this more fun than dealing with all that? And it is, because Rockstar made it that way.

Yes, there are missions. But have you seen the kicks?

There has always been a have-it-both-ways nature to Grand Theft Auto’s satire. Rockstar is happy to facilitate the same American male id it’s lampooning, and the staggering number of copies sold suggests that even conservative commentators out there appealing to incel logic are logging right onto their PlayStations the moment they stop posting. But despite what critics may claim to their audiences, Grand Theft Auto VI’s manosphere parodies are not a huge departure for the series, because the problems with toxic masculinity remain woefully consistent, as do the grifters who seek to profit from it. Insecurity is both a big business and a renewable energy source.

What’s left out of all these complaints about Grand Theft Auto VI being a game where you embody a simp man is that you do not have to do any of the loving behavior these clowns rail against in the video game. You can ignore Lucia when playing as Jason, let your relationship grow distant and decay. You can leave the walls unpainted, never pick up flowers or groceries, not press the button to hold Lucia’s hand, keep your distance on the dance floor. The game just makes clear what the real world does not: That’s a good way to end up alone. And that’s the one thing the parodied blowhards of GTA VI’s in-game manosphere broadcast loud and clear: that they’re alone.

#6694. The Secrets Behind Brittany Snow’s Press-Tour Glow

The actress is embracing a more intentional beauty routine with a little help from RéVive Skincare.

Though her recent red-carpet looks may beg to differ, Brittany Snow is no longer chasing perfection—at least when it comes to her appearance. Instead, the actress, who turned 40 this year and is starring in one of the moment’s most deliciously bingeable series, now in its second season, is focused on aging well and nourishing her skin with intention. “There’s something really freeing about realizing you don’t need to look perfect to feel confident,” Snow says. “I spent so much of my younger years unfortunately being aware of how I looked. Now, I’m much more interested in just looking like myself, just hopefully a little more hydrated.” That’s where RéVive comes in.

Snow credits her makeup artist Charlie Riddle with introducing her to the luxe skin care brand and helping her evolve her relationship to beauty. “He has always focused on making my skin look like skin—healthy, hydrated, and luminous,” she says. “He understands that the better you take care of your skin, the less you need to cover it up.”

Throughout the current press tour, Riddle has been prepping Snow’s skin with RéVive; the brand has quickly become a staple in her personal routine, too. “I was initially drawn to how beautiful my skin felt when Charlie used the products on me,” she says. “There was this sense of hydration without feeling like I had a million things sitting on my face. Charlie has taught me that the edit matters; I used to be someone who thought more products meant better results, and now I realize that consistency and quality are much more important.”

In addition to the products’ elegant feel and innovative, science-based formulas, Snow also appreciates RéVive’s brand story. “RéVive was founded by a plastic surgeon whose research began with helping burn victims heal,” she says. “There’s something really meaningful to me about a beauty brand that was born out of wanting to help people.”

Whether she’s preparing to film a scene, gearing up for a marathon press day, or decompressing before bed at home, she relies on RéVive’s Renewal Moisturizing Night Cream and Renewal Rescue Elixir Oil to hydrate, care for, and rejuvenate her skin.

Both products are powered by exclusive peptides enhanced by RéVive RVGF Technology—a breakthrough delivery system that targets skin concerns with greater precision to maximize efficacy. #6690. The Carnivore Diet Is Peak Protein Extremism. How Healthy Is It Really?

You know your obsession with protein has gone too far when you’re waiting in line at Erewhon for a raw meat smoothie. The speciality drink was created by Paul Saladino, who regularly preaches the benefits of following an animal-based diet. If you look inside the blender, you’ll find kefir, beef organs (like liver, heart, kidney, and spleen from Saldino’s Heart & Soil line), and “immunomilk,” which is freeze-dried cow’s colostrum. Yum. Saladino may be an outlier, but he certainly isn’t the only person pushing a meat-heavy diet. Brian Johnson, aka the “liver king,” follows an extreme ancestral carnivore diet, eating a pound of raw liver a day.

Eating raw organs is a step too far, but maybe you’ve heard about the benefits of the carnivore diet and you’re curious. According to a 2026 study published in Nutrients, the number of posts about the carnivore diet on Instagram is in the millions—and they didn’t even look at TikTok. Interest surrounding the carnivore diet has shown no signs of slowing down.

Maybe plant-based eating leaves you gassy and unsatisfied. You can’t help that you like wings. Before you take vegetables off the table completely, it’s important to know what the carnivore diet is and how it impacts health, both short-term and long-term. As experts explain here, it’s not all bad. But there are some important risks to be aware of.

The aforementioned Nutrients study on the carnivore diet explains that there isn’t one standard definition of what the carnivore diet actually is, but generally speaking, it’s a diet where you only eat minimally processed animal foods, including organ meats, fish, seafood, eggs, animal fats, and full-fat dairy. Plant-based foods are eliminated entirely.

While eliminating foods like fruits, vegetables, and whole grains is extreme, Pouria Sefidmooye Azar, PhD, RD, a registered dietitian and assistant professor at the University of Central Arkansas, says the carnivore diet isn’t all bad. He says that short term, many people lose weight eating this way.

“Protein is more satiating than carbs and fats, so people following the carnivore diet often stay full for a longer amount of time, which means they reduce their caloric intake,” he says. Logically, it makes sense. If you’re eating foods like beef, chicken, and salmon, you’ll be less likely to dig into the pantry for snacks than if you ate a bowl of noodles.

Dr. Azar says it’s important not to conflate weight loss with getting healthier. He says that by eliminating plants, you’re going to miss out on a lot of important nutrients the body needs. You can probably guess the big one. Yep, fiber. “"If you’re cutting out every plant food, you're not getting fiber or phytonutrients, which are protective compounds found only in plants,” says Chris Vogliano, PhD, RD, a registered dietitian and global food systems expert.

While you might not suffer any consequences of this immediately, both dietitians say that continuing to eat this way can mess up your digestion. You need fiber for good poops, plain and simple. Dr. Azar says that we also need fiber to feed the healthy gut bacteria in the microbiome. This is important for supporting mental health, immune health, and minimizing the risk of chronic diseases and cancers.

Dr. Azar specifically calls out the connection between a high-meat, low-fiber diet and the risk of colorectal cancer. For example, a 2015 Oncology Reviews study shows a connection between red meat consumption and colorectal cancer risk, while a 2026 European Journal of Cancer study called low fiber consumption a major risk factor for colorectal cancer.

Considering that men are at increased risk for heart disease (the number one cause of death in the U.S.), it’s important to know how the carnivore diet can impact your cardiovascular health. Spoiler alert: It’s not good. “I would not recommend the carnivore diet as a healthy, long-term eating pattern,” says Sunny Intwala, MD, MBA, preventive cardiologist and the director of Prevention & Wellness at Northwell Health.

Dr. Intwala explains that this is because meat doesn’t just contain protein; it has a lot of saturated fat too. He says that diets centering around red meat increase LDL cholesterol and blood pressure in a few short weeks. This, he says, can contribute to inflammation and plaque buildup that increases the risk of heart attack and stroke.

As someone who studies how the way we eat impacts the planet, Dr. Vogliano points out that the carnivore diet is pretty horrible for the environment. “From a food systems lens, a meat-only diet on a global or even national level would carry massive environmental costs from land, water, and greenhouse gas emissions. This is regardless of whether the meat is conventionally raised, organic, or even regenerative. There’s just not enough land to produce that much meat,” he says.

Okay, we need plants. But what about the Brian Johnsons and Paul Salidinos of the world preaching the benefits of eating raw meat? If you are going to eat meat, are there benefits to eating it raw?

Both dietitians say no, emphasizing that there is no scientific evidence showing that raw meat is more beneficial in any way than eating cooked meat. “Liver is a nutrient-rich food and a great way to get vitamin A, vitamin B12, folate, and iron. But you can get that from cooked liver; you don’t have to eat it raw,” Dr. Vogliano says. In fact, he emphasizes that eating any meat raw increases the risk of foodborne illnesses like Salmonella and E.coli.

Dr. Azar warns against pulling a Rocky and eating raw eggs either. “The protein in raw eggs is between 50 and 60% digestible. But the protein digestibility in cooked eggs is over 90%,” he says. A study from the ‘90s in The Journal of Nutrition backs this up.

It’s worth noting that this isn’t the same for meat. A 2015 study in the same journal found that the cooking time for meat didn’t impact protein digestibility very much. So while you may get the same amount of digestible protein from raw meat as you would cooked meat, your risk of foodborne illness is greater.

Decades of scientific research make it clear that a plant-free diet is not a healthy diet. If you’re a meat lover, you might be wondering just how much meat you can get away with eating without compromising your health.

Dr. Azar’s advice is this: Meat can still be your primary protein source. Just eat some plants along with it. “If you love meat, you can still eat foods like beef and chicken, but you also need to eat fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and nuts and seeds because there are some nutrients you just can’t get from meat,” he says, adding that only eating meat will lead to nutrient deficiencies.

Dr. Vogliano delivers a dietary message you’ve likely heard many times before: The healthiest diet is a diverse one. “We know from scientific research that the more plant foods our diets consist of, the more insurance we have that we’re getting the nutrients the body needs,” he says. Because of this, he advocates for a primarily plant-based diet and only eating meat occasionally.

Different governing bodies have slightly different recommendations when it comes to how much meat you can eat while still maintaining a healthy diet. The American Institute for Cancer Research says to keep red meat under 18 ounces a week, or roughly three portions a week. The American Heart Association doesn’t give a specific serving recommendation for meat, but says to mostly get protein from plants, fish, and seafood.

Dr. Azar emphasizes that there isn’t one universal way of eating that works for everyone. One diet may make one person feel energized and leave someone else feeling exhausted. What is important, he says, is making sure you’re getting all the nutrients your body needs. And what we know for sure is that you can’t do that by just eating meat.

#6684. The New Rules of Complexion Makeup

A decade ago, many of us wouldn’t leave the house without a full-coverage beat. As Instagram selfies and YouTube tutorials took over pop culture, meticulously sculpted, perfected complexions reigned supreme—until the pendulum swung in the opposite direction, ushering in an era of barely-there coverage and skin-care-infused formulas. And while the early 2020s were defined by ultra-dewy, almost damp-looking skin, today’s complexion ideal strikes a more nuanced balance: coverage without the weight, radiance without the shine.

“Modern complexion formulations have come such a long way, and the new-Gen complexion products give medium to buildable coverage that glides and melts into skin, while giving a soft-focus matte finish that reads radiant rather than shiny,” says celebrity makeup artist and Vogue Beauty Board member Fara Homidi. “We can now get more coverage, while the final look is breathable and has flex to it, never heavy and cakey.” Nowadays, lightweight texture, skin-friendly ingredients, and flexible coverage are non-negotiable. The ideal product perfects your complexion without looking or feeling like makeup.

“I want the complexion product to be able to be great, without the help of a concealer or bronzer,” says content creator and fellow Board member Toni Bravo. “It also needs the right undertones that bring out dimension naturally,” she says, to create a second-skin effect.

Mastering your complexion, however, is both the science of formulation and the art of application. While formulas are more advanced than ever, technique and placement have simultaneously evolved. Homidi points out that it’s not about wearing less makeup, but about how it’s placed on the skin. Her best advice is to put the product only where you need it like under the eyes or around the nose, with lighter coverage around the the rest of the face. She prefers pinpointing blemishes and discolorations with fuller coverage, while letting the rest of the skin breathe.

Looking ahead, beauty lovers and experts alike can expect complexion makeup to keep evolving. “Hopefully, complexion products continue to evolve shade-wise,” says Bravo. “We’ve seen brands truly expand the meaning of inclusivity in the last few years, in ways 14-year-old me wouldn’t believe. Folks understanding undertones, and how to apply them to our complexion products, will make for a more conscious consumer and intentional brand.” Meanwhile, Homidi expects further advancements in texture and innovative application methods (roller ball foundation applicator, anyone?). In short, the future looks more inclusive, with advanced formulations and better shade matches for everyone.

Below, a look at some of the latest foundation and skin tint launches that we believe are pushing the category forward; with some helpful insights from the Vogue Beauty Board members who have tested them.

Vogue Beauty Board’s Toni Bravo uses Dior’s Backstage Glow-Up Skin Tint.

I love the glow and the wearability of this skin tint. I prefer a glowy finish, so this one was right up my alley. I have combination skin, so going forward I’d wear this with my favorite mattifying primer to keep it from getting too shiny. I used shade 8N. It pulls fairly neutral, so if you have a warmer undertone, I’d pay close attention to the swatches before applying, especially since it includes SPF.

FROM THE BOARD: Marianna Hewitt, beauty creator and Summer Fridays cofounder

“I love complexion products that still look like skin and what I like about this formula is the natural glow and the ability to build a little more coverage where you want it. It gives your skin a more even look without feeling overly heavy and perfect for light makeup days.”

FROM THE BOARD: Conçetta Ciarlo, beauty shopping writer

I was surprised by how much I liked this skin tint—I’m not usually fond of tints because they tend to look too shiny on my oily skin and don’t provide much coverage. The real draw here was the special attention to shades for neutral undertones (me!). I went with shade 2N, and it was a perfect match—plus, this gave a surprising amount of coverage, blurring away any light hyperpigmentation marks I had. The finish is definitely radiant, but I found it natural and lightweight-feeling. My only hesitation is that the formula isn’t totally non-comedogenic, and I’m acne-prone, so I’d reach for this when my skin is in maintenance mode (AKA clear, and upkeeping that) rather than actively breaking out.

FROM THE BOARD: Kiana Murden, beauty shopping editor

First of all, I love that this is called a ‘tinted cream’—it feels like a modern reimagining of the tinted moisturizer. I tried this for the first time uptown at Violet Grey’s NYC boutique, and was so pleased with the shade match. I couldn’t believe how incredible my skin looked. When I got home, I put the tub front-and-center in my vanity (where I keep the things I reach for most often), and have used it for most makeup days since. Lightweight, sort of gel-like, and hydrating with a natural finish, this is a winner in my book.

Vogue Beauty Board’s Marianna Hewitt uses Carte Blanche’s Multi-Hyphenate.

FROM THE BOARD: Marianna Hewitt, beauty creator and Summer Fridays cofounder

I love formulas that bring skincare and makeup together in a thoughtful way. I like that this combines mineral SPF with brightening ingredients and it has a bit more coverage than a skin tint. FROM THE BOARD: Kiana Murden, beauty shopping editor

If you see me on a stage or at a photoshoot, this is probably the secret to my skin looking good. In fact, I’ve decided to leave it in my beauty closet makeup bag because I get ready for most weekday things from our office. Celebrity makeup artist Hung Vanngo’s serum foundation is easy to love. While many newer formulas are sheer or light coverage, this is medium-to-full. Fortunately it achieves such without the weight—blurring skin without feelign heavy, pilling, or caking. A feat!

Vogue Beauty Board’s Michelle Lee uses TIRTIR’s Tinted Skin Glow Cushion.

FROM THE BOARD: Michelle Lee, K-beauty expert and K-Beauty World CMO

I’m not typically a fan of cushion foundations. I’ve tried the other varieties of the TirTir cushion and never found one that I loved. I have very dry, dehydrated skin, so some cushions can accentuate dry spots, especially if there’s any peeling—but I really loved this one! The finish is dewy without looking oily, and the shade match (23N for me) was spot on. Another big issue with cushions for me has always been the cleanliness of the puff, but I like this formulation so much, I’m committed to a regular puff-washing routine and getting extra puffs to have on hand.
