#6624. The 7 Lessons I Learned About Skin After Losing 85 Pounds

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Plagued by the prospect of excess and loose skin, one writer investigates the surgical and noninvasive options that lie ahead

I lost 85 pounds without bariatric surgery. Weight loss has been on my mind basically my entire life, especially since I started this journey in earnest in July 2019. And, as proud of myself as I most certainly am for losing this weight and finally getting healthier, it is met toe-to-toe with pervasive anxiety and a nagging question: What about excess skin?

Because I’m losing weight more slowly, I haven’t yet encountered loose skin, though I still have at least 50 more pounds to go. I worry, perhaps too much, about whether I’ll make it to my goal weight without needing skin tightening at the end of this journey.

It’s a pretty unsexy topic—which is why it’s rarely, if ever, discussed. But for those like me who are on major weight-loss journeys, or whose bodies have changed significantly through pregnancy, it’s a question that plagues us: Am I going to encounter excess skin the more weight I lose? And if I do, what can I do about it?

Apparently, I’m not the only one with questions, according to New York City plastic surgeon Lara Devgan. “Skin tightening remains one of the elusive black boxes in the world of plastic surgery,” she says. That said, we’re all still learning about best practices—from me to medical professionals.

So I decided to dig deeper. I rounded up five renowned dermatologists and plastic surgeons from across the country and asked them my questions. And here’s what they have to say.

“Losing weight gradually rather than rapidly may prevent excess skin after major weight loss,” says Los Angeles–based dermatologist Harold Lancer. “However, rapid large-scale weight loss will invariably result in excess skin.” Devgan seconds that. “The best way to prevent skin laxity after weight loss is to do your best to lose weight at a slow and steady pace,” she says. “Although it may sound appealing to get to the finish line quickly, that is actually the worst thing you can do in terms of skin laxity.” Losing weight slowly, she says, allows the skin to contract and shrink as the body shape changes.

Though I personally haven’t opted for weight loss surgery, many do—and there is zero shame in that. But because weight is lost more rapidly after surgery, the likelihood of excess skin increases, so experts recommend pairing weight loss surgery with a skin removal procedure. Why worry about excess skin, especially after faster weight loss? It’s “because collagen and elastin fibers are destroyed when skin is stretched significantly and remains stretched for an extended amount of time,” says New York City plastic surgeon David Shafer. “Patients should plan on staged procedures if having a weight loss surgery followed by a skin removal surgery.”

“Typically, younger patients with thicker and more sebaceous skin will have more skin contraction during weight loss due to better elasticity,” Devgan says. “Starting in the 20s, tissue elasticity begins to decline. Even in the absence of weight fluctuation, loss of tissue turgor and decreased firmness can be seen in midface descent in the late 20s, breast laxity in the 30s, abdominal laxity in the 40s, and extremity laxity in the 50s.”

However, Devgan says everyone’s body is different. “There is a tremendous amount of variability in the human experience, so some patients may lose 50 pounds with minimal change in their body, while others can lose as few as 10 and see tissue laxity.” If you are genetically blessed with unusually superb tissue elasticity, Devgan says, it can be less dramatic. (And lucky you.)

Lifestyle choices can also factor in, Boston-based dermatologist Ranella Hirsch says. How long were you at the weight you started losing from? Are you a smoker? Do you spend a lot of time in the sun without protection? All these factors play into skin elasticity.

“Using an emollient moisturizer rich in vitamin E will help improve the barrier protection of the skin and lock in moisture,” Devgan says. She also says the topical medical-grade ingredients you use on your face for firmness and tightness—like hyaluronic acid, peptides, niacin, squalene, vitamins C and B, retinol, and bakuchiol—can work elsewhere, too. “Most people focus on using these for the face and neck in their daily routines, but from a molecular perspective, their efficacy is present anywhere on the body.” But save your money on creams that promise you the world. “Losing large amounts of weight rapidly tends to leave skin behind,” Hirsch says. “Though creams with incredible claims abound, they actually do little.”

Nécessaire The Body Lotion with Niacinamide

Biossance Squalane + Caffeine Toning Body Cream

Sol de Janeiro Bom Dia Bright Body Cream with Vitamin C

U Beauty The SCULPT Arm Compound Body Serum

Building muscle through weight training might help reduce the appearance of lax skin, New York City dermatologist Dendy Engelman says. “This helps reduce the appearance by replacing the lost fat with muscle mass.”

Nonsurgical options can help with loose skin after weight loss, but they won’t help with skin folds or hanging skin. “Noninvasive treatments such as laser and radiofrequency can help tighten the skin, but there is a limit to how much they can do,” Shafer adds. “Hanging skin generally needs to be surgically excised with procedures such as abdominoplasty, body lift, and arm lift.” Shafer says there’s a difference between loose skin and hanging skin. “It’s possible patients can manage and treat excess skin cases without undergoing skin removal surgery, such as if the skin is loose but not hanging.” He adds, “In that case, noninvasive treatments may be useful, but hanging skin most often requires surgical excision.”

“After major weight loss, people may have skin that hangs off their body,” Engelman says. “These heavy folds can cause health problems such as pain, inflammation, and frequent infections from the skin constantly rubbing together. This can happen during exercise or everyday activities. When a person is having functional issues because of their excess skin, it should be a sign that this problem needs to be addressed.” And, of course, everyone’s journey is different.

Lancer says some individuals will tolerate moderate laxity and be happy with the weight-loss accomplishment; others will seek skin tightening for as little as a five-pound weight loss. But, he says, if plastic surgery does become the option on the table, “I would recommend getting at least three opinions from doctors who exclusively do excess body skin reduction. Once you select a doctor, do one small area on your body, so you can evaluate the procedure, how your body heals, and your results. Afterward, you can determine whether you’d like to proceed with a full-blown larger procedure.”

He suggests consulting a dermatologist for nonsurgical options, then asking that doctor to recommend plastic surgeons who specialize in excess body skin reduction if you feel that is the right path for you. This is a major decision and shouldn’t be taken lightly. Bring medical professionals along for the entire weight-loss journey (even if you’ve already started) and ask all the questions: Which specific procedure is best? How much will it cost? Will insurance cover it? (From my research so far, no, if it is cosmetic, but perhaps yes if it would help correct something that limits your daily functionality.) No question is off-limits, and don’t try to make these decisions alone.

If this piece applies to you at all, whether it’s longstanding weight you carried, weight you lost during pregnancy, or somewhere in between, that means one thing: You’ve taken major steps toward better physical health, and that should be applauded. “Everyone’s weight loss story is different, and some days are harder than others,” Engelman says. “I say, try to be kind to yourself. You’ve just reached a huge accomplishment and should be proud of that.”

Devgan agrees. “Accomplishing a personal health goal like major weight loss is an incredible achievement that anyone should be proud of,” she says. “While excess skin can feel like a burden or source of self-consciousness, it is also a reminder of the metaphorical and literal shedding of the weight of a prior version of oneself. You cannot have a couture gown without a seam, and you cannot have a surgery without a scar. Life has limitations, but that does not make it less beautiful. It makes it more real.”

A Copenhagen apartment delivers Scandinavian style up close. Think herringbone floors, tall windows, blonde wood, and a kitchen that’s set up to actually cook in. #6618. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6616. Why Weed Might Actually Be Bad for Your Sleep

Everyone’s done it before. A pre-game gummy. A nighttime toke. Weed is, at this point, a widely used sleep aid. It usually works pretty well, too. But if you’ve made it a habit, you might just be sabotaging your shut-eye in the long run. According to a new October 2026 study, consuming pot in any form before bed causes people to have poorer quality of sleep—without them even realizing it. In other words: It has exactly the opposite of its intended effect. Here’s what you should know before popping an edible before you doze off.

The study, which was performed by Northwestern University researchers and published in JAMA Network, looked at 1,266 adults who participated in the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, which followed participants for 35 years to determine how behavioral, biological, and environmental factors affected their risk of heart disease later in life. Of that sample size, 891 wore wrist-based activity monitors for at least a week so that researchers could examine their sleep patterns. After analyzing the data, the researchers found that those who were long-term cannabis users had “poorer objective sleep, including lower sleep efficiency, greater fragmentation, and more time awake during the night,” Dr. Thanh-Huyen Vu, an author of the study and a research associate professor of preventive medicine at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, tells GQ.

Here’s what all of that means: Sleep efficiency is essentially how much of the time you spend in bed you’re actually asleep. So, lower sleep efficiency means spending more time lying awake instead of sleeping while sleep fragmentation refers to how often your sleep is interrupted, like when you’re unknowingly tossing and turning to get comfortable. The researchers also looked at how much total time participants spent awake during the night. It all boils down to the fact that long-term cannabis users weren’t sleeping as soundly or as continuously throughout the night—sometimes without them even knowing it.

The researchers can’t say for certain. Because the study was observational, it only established an association between long-term cannabis exposure and poorer sleep quality.

One possibility, Vu suggests, is that cannabis may “alter normal sleep architecture,” potentially changing the way the body cycles through different sleep stages.

Over time, it’s those changes that can contribute to more nighttime awakenings, which result in less restorative sleep. She says more research is needed to understand the underlying biological mechanisms.

Deep sleep is one of the most important stages of sleep because it’s the phase when your body recovers physically, processes memory, and regulates the immune system. Interruptions in sleep result in less time during the deep sleep cycle, which inhibits your body from doing all the important things that help you function properly when you’re awake. The less deep sleep you get, the worse you feel in the morning. The reason why participants don’t pick up on these mid-sleep wake-ups is that they’re easy to forget. “Sleep trackers can capture some of these patterns, even when people don’t perceive their sleep as being particularly poor,” Vu says. It’s the same way in which you think you slept eight hours one night but woke up feeling groggy regardless.

Not necessarily. Given the sample population—middle-aged adults—the results may not apply to people in other age ranges or even those who use cannabis for medical reasons. Still, Vu says it’s important for people to understand that cannabis’s relationship with sleep may be more complicated than simply helping you drift off faster.

If you regularly use cannabis before bed, paying attention to your sleep patterns may help you better understand how it’s affecting you. Wearable sleep trackers can offer some insight into nighttime awakenings and sleep efficiency, but you won’t get the same sleep analysis if you were part of a study like this. It might be worth trying out a period where you don’t use weed to fall asleep to see if it makes a difference in whether you feel more well-rested, or your mind feels sharper. Though the study still leaves a lot of questions to be answered, its data is clear enough to make anyone with a nightly gummy habit reconsider.

#6614. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6612. The Tucson Restaurant Turning Cactus Into Fine Dining

Traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat. Plants armed with burs, barbs, and spines all but scream “do not touch.” For chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee, however, this prickly, dusty landscape stocks a pantry of possibility. The married co-owners of Ursa see the Arizona desert as a rich ground for foraging.

Gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake. Dusty, sage-colored salt bush, when hung to dry, takes on an intensely umami, aquatic saltiness like seaweed. The sweet buds of the Seussian-green palo verde tree become briny, like olives, when suffused with lye.

Don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year. The restaurant processes the young and mature paddles, fruit and their seeds, buds, and flowers, which are then grilled, poached, cold-smoked, juiced, dehydrated, nixtamalized, or preserved into jam, wine, and vinegar.

There are hundreds of edible plants in the Sonoran Desert. Ursa strives to showcase their potential, one 10-course meal at a time.

“We treat Ursa as an art showroom, demonstrating to people what these plants can do, what sustainable means, and what was here before it got easy,” says Lopez. The idea was inspired in part by his Sonoran grandfather, Hector Lopez, who died in the spring. “He was the first person I ever heard say they’re proud to be from the desert,” the chef said.

Ursa began as a pop-up in California in 2023. Lopez and Chee moved to a historic brick building in downtown Tucson, re-opening their doors in October 2025. It’s a homecoming of sorts for the couple, who are both from the Sonoran Desert borderlands. They met in Hawaii, where Chee was working in clean energy and transportation. Lopez, meanwhile, spent roughly 18 years cooking in fine dining and modern progressive restaurants like Redbird and Orsa & Winston in LA, and Pai Honolulu. But he was longing for the desert.

After helping a friend open a restaurant and hosting a few popups in Austin, Lopez and Chee bought a desert foraging guide, packed up their two dogs and began driving around the Southwest. It made sense to settle in Tucson, which was recognized by UNESCO in 2015 as a Creative City of Gastronomy for its continuous 4,000-year agricultural history and deeply rooted Sonoran Desert food traditions.

“That’s a unique thing about being here, the connection from seed to plant to restaurant that we hadn’t been able to grasp before,” Chee says.

Consider a recent course that Ursa built around tepary beans, in which the ancient, nutty bean is refried and topped with h:al squash that’s been lactofermented. The squash’s leaves are fermented to make Japanese-style kosho and its flowers are pickled, dried, crushed with dried saltbush, then tossed with barrel cactus seeds for a desert furikake. It’s served with grilled coins of chorizo made from Lopez’s great-grandmother’s recipe and housemade flour tortillas, to all be washed down with an amazake drink made from fermented wheat and goat fat. Don’t get too attached, however. Riffs owing to finicky ingredient availability occur here almost daily.

Running a restaurant using only ingredients foraged and farmed from within about eight to 10 miles means abiding by pretty intense guardrails. The only wheat used is pima club, an ancient soft white variety cultivated for centuries by the Akimel O’odham (Pima) people. Ursa does not use cucumbers, radishes or citrus.

“We’re not trying to substitute anything, like, ‘How do we achieve cucumber? Let’s grab a cactus,’” Lopez says. “We have to throw everything out, really strip it down. Sometimes we have to let the ingredients be bitter or spicy. We have to put our egos aside and let the ingredient be the star.”

For staff who didn’t grow up or learn to cook here, the learning curve at Ursa can feel a little like alighting on a new planet, even if certain flora happen to resemble prickly weeds in their own backyards.

“We have these really cool moments in the restaurant where people are like, Oh! I have lamb’s quarter just growing in my yard!” Chee says of the spinach-like desert green that appears all over Ursa’s menu.

A young Aaron Lopez with his grandfather Hector Lopez.

Ursa’s approach isn’t always easy for customers to understand, so the couple came up with a more down-to-earth option. This fall, the restaurant debuted a four-course, family-style Lineage menu for $75, alongside the existing 10-course Harvest menu ($150). There’s now a pozole course inspired by the family’s annual springtime tradition of roasting goat in agave leaves, barbacoa-style, and shredding it for soup, and a red masa tamal with glazed quail and yucca blossoms in mole made with burnt mesquite bread, a technique Lopez remembers from childhood.

The idea took shape during Ursa’s extended summer break, as Lopez recovered from foot surgery and reflected on the loss of his late grandfather, the tenacious keeper of family traditions.

“I feel so much closer to my ancestors and the land; we want Ursa to be less esoteric and more soulful,” he says. “The story of Ursa is partly of the desert, partly my family. Now we’ve advanced to the point where they’re symbiotic, and I can't tell them apart.”

#6611. Should You Worry About That Bump on Your Chest?

If you’re like most guys, you probably have plenty of little bumps and lumps on your skin. There’s the callus on your toe from training for that 10K, the razor bumps along your neck from this morning’s shave, and the skin tag on your underarm you keep meaning to get removed. While it’s often completely fine to ignore these bumps, that isn’t always the case. Some can be a red flag worth paying attention to—especially if they’re on your chest.

While male breast cancer is rare, estimates suggest that more than 2,600 men are diagnosed with an invasive form of the disease each year in the United States, and more than 500 die, according to the American Cancer Society. And one of its telltale signs is a firm bump under or near your nipple. Below, find out more about what a breast-cancer lump may look like and four other things that could be to blame for a new bump on your chest.

There isn’t a universal description of what breast cancer lumps look like in men, but there are some common characteristics to keep in mind. “Breast cancer in men typically presents as a painless, firm, or hard lump,” says Jose Pablo Leone, MD, the director of the Program for Breast Cancer in Men at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston.

Another sign that the bump could be breast cancer is if it’s behind or very close to the nipple and areola. “Men have much less developed breast glandular tissue than women, which is why breast cancer in men most commonly develops near or behind the nipple,” says Dr. Leone. As for size even a lump as small as a pea can be cancerous, but by the time men go to the doctor, tumors are often larger than a marble, according to Dr. Leone. “In part because of the lack of awareness and screening, most men present with larger tumors,” he says. “But any size is worth mentioning to your doctor. Not all breast cancers feel the same, so any new or persistent breast lump should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.”

Your chest has a lot of oil glands, which can set the stage for pimples. “Staying in a sweaty shirt after a workout can make chest acne flare, especially if the fabric is tight and rubs against your skin,” says Elizabeth Bahar Houshmand, MD, a board-certified dermatologist based in Dallas. While blackheads and whiteheads are typically small and easy to identify, inflamed pimples or nodules may seem more alarming because they can be hard, painful, and form deep under the skin. When it comes to nodular acne specifically, you can’t treat it on your own. If that’s what you think you’re dealing with, see a dermatologist, who can prescribe an oral or topical medication to help clear it up.

“This is a collection of fat that forms under the skin,” says Sonya Kenkare, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at Illinois Dermatology Institute in Hinsdale, Illinois. “It is usually soft, not painful, and you can move it around in all different directions.” You don’t need to do anything about a lipoma, but if you want to get it removed, you can talk to a doctor about it.

When hair follicles get inflamed or infected, you can end up with folliculitis. “Folliculitis often looks like small pimples or pus-filled bumps centered around a hair follicle” says Dr. Houshmand. “They may itch or feel tender.”

Blockage or damage to a hair follicle can also cause epidermal inclusion cysts. These cysts occur when dead skin cells get trapped under the surface instead of shedding. “They feel somewhat firm and often have a central little black spot,” says Dr. Kenkare. Sometimes simply applying a warm compress to the area can help a cyst heal on its own, but a doctor can also inject it with a steroid to reduce swelling, drain it, or surgically remove it.

This condition occurs when breast tissue gets enlarged in men, and it can first appear as a lump under your nipple. “It often feels like a rubbery or firm disc beneath the nipple, and it may be tender,” says Dr. Houshmand. While gynecomastia can come on as a side effect of some medications, like antibiotics or antidepressants, or diseases like thyroid disorders, sometimes there is no clear cause at all.

If you’re starting to feel like it’s difficult to tell on your own what the lump on your chest might be, you’re not wrong. That’s why it’s best to have your primary care physician look at any new, unexplained bumps and tell you whether you need imaging, like a mammogram with an ultrasound. That may sound scary, but it’s really just covering your bases. “Uncommon things are uncommon, and breast cancer in men is uncommon,” says Dr. Leone. “You shouldn’t worry excessively about male breast cancer, but you should be aware of it.”

#6610. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6608. How Women Weavers Are Preserving Indigenous Amazigh Culture in Morocco

Malika Oubzou is sitting on a red and blue handwoven rug on the floor of her childhood home in Tamda Noumercid, a small village near Azilal in Morocco’s Atlas Mountains. The 36-year-old weaving artisan is enjoying a glass of milk and a plump, juicy date from a large plate she’s set out for guests—myself among them—when she looks up to see even more people arriving. To accommodate the new visitors, she finishes her milk, leaves the room, and returns with a low table. Then another. And another after that.

Soon enough, more food comes out: a steaming clay pot of tajine maazi (goat tagine) with potatoes and carrots, fresh tomato salad, and fluffy Tafarnout bread, still warm from the clay oven. Malika shifts the tables around to make room for the additional food, and her brother, Mohammed, rearranges the pillows that line the rug-filled floors of the space. It continues like this for the next couple of hours: A table appears here, a pillow moves there. Food comes in and food goes out. The only thing that stays put? The rugs themselves.

Malika Oubzou greets her neighbors at the door of her home in Azilal. In Morocco, Friday is celebrated as "Couscous Day," a cherished tradition where families gather for a communal lunch, usually after the weekly congregational prayer.

“In a typical rural Moroccan household, everything is mobile except the rugs,” Jihane Lahbibi, the Moroccan co-founder of the Moroccan rug brand Casa Amar, tells me as we dunk our Tafarnout into the tagine juices. “The pillows, tables, mattresses…they are all roving. But the rugs are the constant. Symbolically, they are the pillars. They anchor the room. They are the room.” In fact, as Malika echoes later through a translator, rugs are the most sacred part of the home. “When you welcome guests,” she says, “the rug is everything.”

Malika was the first weaver Jihane and her Italian husband Matteo met when they began looking for artisans to make custom rugs for Casa Amar back in 2021. Today, they partner with women in five communities across Morocco to create and source rugs for clients across the world, and were even part of Milan Design Week last year. As interest in Moroccan craftsmanship and design continues to soar, I’ve come to spend some time with a few of the artisans Jihane and Matteo work with to learn more about the Amazigh weaving culture behind the craft.

This scene with the roving tables is a very good start. It’s impossible to miss the deep significance of rugs in everyday Moroccan life once you experience their starring role in every room, after all. But as the days go by, I realize rugs have taken on even more meaning in recent decades, too: They’ve become a way to keep Amazigh culture alive in the face of modernization.

“Younger generations aren’t making as many rugs these days, so when the older women weavers eventually die, the younger ones won’t know how to make them—and that makes me really, really sad,” Malika tells me after we’ve finished our tagine and have moved on to mint tea and a bowl of grapes for dessert. “So now, when I’m weaving, I think about my culture. I also think about the satisfaction of making something good, and the money I will get from making it. All of those things are important. But rugs are objects that last, and because they last, they are one of the best ways to preserve the culture.”

Like most Indigenous traditions around the world, Moroccan rug weaving dates back thousands of years. Amazigh women (also known as Berber) in the Atlas Mountains originally crafted handknotted rugs from local sheep’s wool to protect themselves and their families from the elements: harsh sun during the day, and freezing mountain temperatures at night. Over time, rug weaving morphed into an art form as well, one filled with all sorts of storytelling and symbolism. Some rug patterns represent universal emotions like love and hope, while others are more like talismans, meant to protect against evil and infertility. No matter the pattern, though, the weaving tradition itself has never been written down anywhere. It’s passed down from mother to daughter simply by watching.

Nejma Oubzou prepares freshly harvested dwarf palm by cutting the thorns off and separating the fan-like leaves in order to dry them out. The fibers are used to create woven items such as baskets, mats, and home decor.

“Amazigh women know how to make rugs the same way many other people around the world know how to make bread…it’s just a part of the culture from a very young age,” Jihane, who grew up in Casablanca, tells me one afternoon as we’re driving through the mountains. “It’s not like someone sits you down on the loom and says, ‘This is how you do it.’ It’s just that you learn the same way you learn how to walk: No one tells you, you just learn it by seeing.” When she started Casa Amar in 2021 after leaving her job as a business lawyer, she used to ask the artisans she met when, exactly, they learned to weave for the first time. But now she’s come to understand that seeking out that information was always a fool’s errand. “I realize now that it was never so specific,” she reflects. “It was always: They’re around, they see, and they try.”

That’s exactly what happened with Malika. She wove her first rug at age 15 after years of watching her mom weave, and then watching her weave some more. But that first rug she ultimately created wasn’t just a result of growing up around looms; it was a way for her to care for her own mind. When she was 10, her older brother asked her to drop out of school. Their sister had just gotten married, their parents worked outside the home in agriculture, and he and his younger brother wanted to stay in school—so he decided Malika would be the one to stay home and handle the household chores. Weaving became her creative outlet as a result. “What happened was that after I finished my household work, I had this emptiness that I wanted to fill, and weaving was how I filled it,” she tells me. “I didn’t go to school and I didn’t work, so weaving was how I took care of my brain. I used it to fill a void.”

Today, Malika continues to weave to fulfill her creative dreams, and to make money by doing so. She works independently in the home, not as part of one of the thousands of weaving cooperatives scattered throughout Morocco. When she’s weaving a custom rug for Casa Amar, she follows the design given to her by their clients. But when she’s weaving just for herself or her family (which is increasingly rare due to her growing amount of paid work), her patterns are instinctive and intuitive, usually based on how she is feeling in the moment. “There’s no particular reasoning behind so many of my designs; it’s just what I like and what my mind tells me to do,” she explains. “It’s a very free process. It’s not like if you have green, you have to put yellow. You can do whatever you want. It’s all in the mind when you’re making a rug for yourself.”

But aside from earning a living and expressing her creativity, there’s a third reason Malika weaves: a desire to preserve her craft in the face of modernization. This is where things get slightly complicated because, in some ways, the tradition is thriving. As any design aficionado knows, the allure of Moroccan textiles is increasingly global and well-documented, everywhere from Instagram to the pages of this very magazine. According to the international research firm 6W, the Moroccan rug market is projected to reach $485 million in the US by 2032, up from $371 million in 2025.

Every step of the wool preparation process is done by hand. After the wool is sheared from the animal, the artisans wash, brush, and spin it into yarn.

New York-based interior designer Sarah Lederman believes this uptick in interest could be a response to, take a guess, AI. “People are craving more handmade items in their homes now because they’re the opposite of uniform,” she says, “and Moroccan rugs bear the mark of the person who made them.” They’re a reminder, in other words, of what it means to be human.

Khadija Rhandouss in the carpet section of the weekly souk in Khmisset. Rhandouss is a local businesswoman who trades in Moroccan rugs. Every Tuesday she attends the weekly souk in Khmisset where all the best rug deals happen before sunrise.

At the same time, there are threats to the longevity of traditional rugmaking. For one thing, as Malika mentioned at multiple points throughout my visit, fewer young women are actually learning the traditional weaving techniques required to make said rugs. The work is time-consuming, after all, and the money isn’t always great. And now that there are more profitable career options available elsewhere, many younger women are choosing to leave their villages in the mountains, making weaving less of an obvious path than it once was.

Nejma Oubzou spins wool into yarn at her home in the Atlas Mountains in Morocco.

That’s not to mention the modern technology that has changed the game even more. In the early 2000s, some Moroccan small producers started to buy machines from China that allowed them to process bad-quality wool (known locally as “dead wool”) to make carpets. While starting a new rug used to begin with cutting pure wool from sheep, these machines—which are still used by many today—make it easy to cut out that step entirely. This eliminates a huge and significant part of the process. “A lot of people think that making a carpet is just about weaving on a loom, but actually, making the raw material—i.e., transforming it from sheep to the wool that allows you to start weaving—is just as important,” Ibrahim Noubl, a longtime Moroccan rug dealer, told me in Marrakech at the beginning of my trip. He owns Soufny Art Gallery on the edge of the medina, and often collaborates with the beloved, art-filled hotel El Fenn just a two-minute walk down the road. “In Morocco, we are very sentimental people. We believe in lots of non-material ideas, like the thought that wool is blessed,” he explained. “When blessed wool is inside your home, it will bring you comfort and joy—but all of that disappears when it’s not alive in the first place.”

Mimouna Fadil attaches the wool to a wooden plank to start a new rug at her home in Khmisset.

Artisans, particularly from the Amazigh communities, hand-dye the wool using traditional techniques, often boiling it with ingredients to create long-lasting, eco-friendly colors. Red wool in Moroccan rug making is traditionally achieved using natural dyes derived from plants, minerals, and insects to produce vibrant, lasting colors. Earthy reds often come from henna or madder root, while brighter shades are created with pomegranate peels or cochineal insects.

With that in mind, vintage rugs are one of the best bets for high-quality wool, Ibrahim advises, because the product has already survived a few decades—so you know the wool is good. (Carpets made from “dead wool” often start to smell after a few years.) But to keep the ancient traditions alive in a competitive marketplace, companies like Casa Amar, Salam Hello, and the ever-popular Beni Rugs also sell new rugs and put traditional, sustainable craftsmanship front and center. Not only do they use high-grade natural wool (no “dead wool” to be found here), but they also work directly with artisans like Malika, helping provide an income that allows them to continue their traditional and beloved craft.

Nejma Oubzou, mother of Malika, in her bedroom in her home in the Atlas Mountains. Her name means “stars.”

Many of the artisans even pray before they sit down at the loom because it’s such a sacred act. They start with the Arabic phrase “Bismillah,” which means “in the name of God,” then follow it up with a prayer for peace and serenity during their time on the loom, often including phrases like nsaliw l mensej f salam ou l hna: “We started with peace; may we finish with peace.” After all, as Jihane tells me at various points over the course of our week together, a rug can be both sacred and a source of income. The two are not mutually exclusive. “To buyers, rugs may be just random objects, but people pray before making them, even for people they don’t know,” she says one Friday over Friday couscous, a longtime weekly tradition in Morocco. “I never want to romanticize weaving, because at the end of the day, artisans make the rugs to survive. But both can be true. Just because you have to earn money doesn’t mean you don’t make it respectfully the way your elders did it. It’s something you do with dignity and pride…something to carry the legacy.”

For the last leg of my Morocco trip, Jihane takes me to Khemisset, a small market town about an hour’s drive inland from the capital Rabat, where she lives with Matteo and their two (adorable) young sons. Khemisset is known for its surrounding countryside—think rolling wheat fields, fragrant eucalyptus trees, and grazing sheep—plus its Amazigh weaving traditions, particularly its regionally specific palm mats. Not many artisans make these mats anymore except those in the Khemisset countryside and a few others scattered throughout the Atlas Mountains, and they are sadly going extinct as a result—so I wanted to see them before it’s too late. Jihane and Matteo are also trying to help preserve the mats by spreading the word to their customers. “It’s simple: If people know about them and buy them, artisans will keep making them,” she tells me in the car on the drive from Rabat.

Unlike handknotted rugs, these palm mats are woven from dried palm leaves (not wool) and embroidered with colorful wool patterns on top. They typically cost much less than wool rugs because the raw material is cheaper, but they’re equally difficult to make—and a bit harder on the hands. The leaves tend to dry out during the day, even after the artisans boil them for softness and place them in sachets. As a result, the six women I meet—all of whom collaborate with Jihane and Matteo—often weave late into the night when it’s cooler, or in the morning before the sun becomes too strong. Despite these challenging conditions, they love what they do and are determined to keep the craft alive. (Not entirely unrelated, they are also determined to stuff me and Jihane with more dates, milk, Tafarnout bread, olive oil, and honey—the welcome spread of choice throughout our journey.)

Nora Rhandouss, Khadija Rhandouss, and Jihane share mint tea in Khadija’s salon in Khmisset.

“The techniques to make these mats are very old and very ancestral,” 60-year-old Fatiha Amalou, one of the artisans, tells me as we snack on a bowl of particularly glistening dates. We are sitting on a green and white patterned rug on the floor of another artisan’s house, where we’ve all gathered to chat. Not surprisingly, we’re also circled around a low table that, wouldn’t you know, magically appeared when we arrived. “The mats are so sacred that back in the old days, when people would die, we would wrap them up in them to take them away for burial,” Fatiha continues. “They were like a cape.”

Today, she is dedicated to preserving that sacred weaving tradition. But she also cares deeply about the craftsmanship itself. “Of course I want the legacy to continue; everyone wants the legacy to continue,” she tells me. “But really, perhaps more than anything else, I want to make something that makes me proud. We always say: If you make a good thing, it means you have a good head.” Another artisan, 51-year-old Khadija Rhandouss, nods in agreement. “When I make something good, I feel at peace,” she says. I tell them all that, as a bit of a perfectionist myself, I can relate to that sentiment wholeheartedly. Fatiha just laughs and smiles. “Yes, weaving is what we need to do to make money,” she says, “but it’s also part of what we do to feel good. It’s part of who we are.”

#6607. How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time

If you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds. The only ingredients are time and heavy cream. You can use an electric mixer, a whisk, or a mason jar and strong-armed devotion.

In whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop. Desserts like Strawberry Eton Mess or Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake fare best with silky, unsweetened, soft-peaked whip. Others, like this show-stopping Berries and Cream Mille-Feuille, gain structure from sturdier peaks.

To make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk. You can also use a handheld mixer or a mason jar and some elbow grease (more on that later).

If you’re opting for a bowl-and-whisk combo, choose your tools wisely. Cream roughly doubles in volume as you whip it, so use a bowl with three to four times the capacity of your liquid. A large balloon whisk, rather than a narrow sauce whisk, helps incorporate plenty of air into the cream.

Be strategic in the dairy aisle too. Heavy cream and heavy whipping cream contain at least 36% milk fat and can be used interchangeably. Skip anything labeled simply “whipping cream”—or, heaven forbid, “light cream”—which contains less fat and won’t hold its loft as well.

For a basic batch, start with 1 cup cold heavy cream, which makes about 2 cups whipped cream. For lightly sweetened whipped cream, add 1 Tbsp. powdered sugar; for vanilla whipped cream, add ½ tsp. vanilla extract or paste.

With your equipment and ingredients in hand, there are only five steps and infinite possibilities.

Because whipped cream is usually eaten with or as dessert, you might not need to sweeten it at all. To keep flavors balanced, we tend to serve whipped cream au naturel with Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie or Diner-Style Rice Pudding.

But there are no hard-and-fast rules. Maybe you love sweetened whipped cream, or you’re serving it with something less sugary—like, say, a bowl of tart blackberries and torn mint leaves.

For lightly sweetened whipped cream, start with about 1 Tbsp. sugar per cup of cream. Powdered sugar dissolves easily and contains a little stabilizer (usually cornstarch), which can lend the whipped cream some extra holding power. Some cooks prefer the cleaner flavor of granulated sugar, which takes a little longer to dissolve. Either way, add the sugar before you start whipping.

If you’re gazing at a bowl of fluffy, ethereal whip and thinking, “Could I make this even more enchanting?” the answer is yes. There are two primary ways to make flavored whipped cream: infuse or stir.

Kitchen professionals and advance planners tend to cold-infuse. Combine your cream with flavorings like rice (for a creamy Horchata) or bourbon (to take a classic pumpkin pie over the top), then store it in the fridge anywhere from three hours to overnight. Strain out any solids before whipping.

You can also add simple flavorings, like vanilla extract, a small splash of liqueur, cocoa, ground spices, citrus zest, or coffee syrup, before you start whipping. For heavier or chunky additions, such as toasted nuts or chopped chocolate, use a rubber spatula to gently fold them in once the cream is whipped.

Peaks are the shape your whipped cream takes when you pull the whisk out of the bowl and hold it upright like the Statue of Liberty’s torch.

Soft peaks are cloudlike and slump over when you lift the whisk. Stiff peaks stand upright and hold their shape. Somewhere in between are medium peaks, which have enough structure to hold a shape while remaining soft and supple.

Most Bon Appétit recipes, such as these Mix-and-Match Fools, involve whipping cream to soft peaks. That velvety texture is our go-to when we’re dolloping whipped cream atop pecan pie.

But we aren’t always such softies. Medium peaks help this Ginger-Raspberry Icebox Cake keep its shape. And old-fashioned chocolate mousse involves whipping batches of cream into stiff and soft peaks: The former is folded into the chocolate mixture for structure, while the softer stuff tops the dessert.

By hand: Our preferred method, whipping cream by hand requires the most time and effort, but it also gives you optimal control over its final texture. Even if you use a mixer to get your whipped cream started, switching to a whisk for the final few moments makes it easier to stop exactly where you want.

In a Mason jar: No whisk? No mixer? No problem. To make whipped cream with your bare hands, put a container with a tight-fitting lid, large mason jar, or leak-proof cocktail shaker into the freezer for five minutes. Get the heavy cream very cold and make sure you have ample headspace in your vessel of choice. About one cup of liquid in a four-cup container is a good amount.

Secure the lid and shake it like you mean it. For the creamiest results, a consistently assertive pace is better than intermittent spurts of brute force. When the liquid stops sloshing and starts feeling and sounding heavier, open the lid and take a peek. If it looks underwhipped, close it back up and keep shaking.

Good news for meal preppers: You can make whipped cream hours in advance. Err on the side of underwhipping it during your prep. Store the lightly whipped cream, covered, in the fridge for up to four hours before serving, then give it a few energetic whisks to bring back its bounce right before you dollop it onto dessert.

You can also freeze whipped cream (no, seriously). It takes a bit of effort, though. Line a baking sheet with parchment, then pipe or scoop spoonfuls of whipped cream onto it. Freeze until the whipped cream nuggets are solid, then peel them off the parchment and store them in an airtight bag in the freezer for one to two months. When you’re ready to serve, let them thaw at room temperature for about 15 minutes.

Instant vanilla pudding is the key to luscious, long-lasting whipped cream.

Need it to hold up longer? Instant vanilla pudding mix is one of BA’s favorite shortcuts for stabilized whipped cream. For every cup of heavy cream, add 1 Tbsp. instant vanilla pudding mix (call it pastry cream powder if anyone gives you sass) and 2 tsp. powdered sugar, then whip as usual. The modified starch in the pudding mix absorbs excess moisture and helps prevent the cream from separating, keeping it fluffy for up to 24 hours.

For something tangier, sour cream adds both flavor and body. Our Pecan Cream Pie whisks ¼ cup sour cream into 1 cup heavy cream; the sour cream cuts the richness while helping the topping hold its shape.

In any case, your dinner party guests don’t have to sit quietly as you furiously whisk their dessert topping to order. Prep work never tasted so sweet.

If your whip isn’t coming together quite right, don’t fret. Simple solutions abound.

This is probably a temperature issue. Cold cream whips more readily and holds onto the air you’re incorporating more effectively, so it comes together faster—and stays fluffy longer. Pop the bowl, whisk, and cream back into the freezer for five minutes, or into the fridge for up to 30. Once everything is cold, resume whisking.

Another possible culprit is the fat content of your cream. Opt for heavy whipping cream or heavy cream over half-and-half or other heavy cream substitutes.

If the cream is just a little too stiff or starting to look grainy, add a splash of chilled heavy cream and slowly whisk it in. Add more, a little at a time, until the texture smooths out.

Keep a close eye on it: If you whisk for too long, you’ll end up with a bowl of butter.

Editor’s note: This story was originally published in 2017 by Julia Black. It has been substantially updated with new reporting and additional advice from the Bon Appétit archives, including contributions by Amiel Stanek, Christina Chaey, Rochelle Bilow, and Elyssa Goldberg.

#6606. How Did This 14-Year-Old Get Sam Bankman-Fried on the Phone?

Journalists who’ve been anxious about losing their jobs to artificial intelligence would be wise to focus on a different, altogether less menacing but equally impressive threat: 14-year-old Eli Goldfine, the shoestring podcaster from Westchester County who last week conducted a 90-minute interview with Sam Bankman-Fried, who’s currently serving a 25-year sentence in federal prison for orchestrating a multi-billion-dollar cryptocurrency grift.

So how, exactly, does this precocious ninth grader with braces—and not a reporter from one of the scores of legacy publications who’d surely be gunning for access to the disgraced cryptocurrency king—score an interview so coveted? “I had written about Sam on Twitter a little bit, and it got picked up by the person who was at the time running Sam’s account,” Goldfine, who hosts a podcast about prediction markets called The Supercycle, told me earlier this week. “I think they were impressed with my knowledge of various parts of his criminal case.”

Goldfine’s classmates are impressed, too, even though he’s been on the receiving end of some gentle ribbing about his on-air ad reads. But can any of them say they got Bankman-Fried to speculate on the likelihood that AI will bring about the extinction of the human race? ("Less than 50%, more than 10%," by the way). Before school’s out for Thanksgiving break, Goldfine joined GQ to talk about his media diet, dream interview subject, and the mechanics of interviewing a man behind bars.

Eli Goldfine: Wait, just to step back here. Are you printing what I'm going to say, or is this just for you to know? It's not a video on the site, right?

Okay. So my podcast is primarily about prediction markets and other broader markets. And I got into that during the 2024 election. My dad showed me Polymarket and I thought, "Wow, this is really cool. It's people staking money on different sides of an outcome. And when you put all that price signal together, it converges on a really accurate probability of a given event happening. How could I investigate this more?" So I learned more about it and I started trading on a fake-money version of Polymarket.

It's called Manifold Markets. And what's cool about that one is, anyone can create their own question rather than the platform deciding. And anyway, I got really into it and then I was like, “I'll write a couple articles about this because I have some ideas.” And then I started doing interviews and it all kind of came out from that.

I think sports betting, like FanDuel and DraftKings—this stuff obviously serves very little utility because it's just the company offering these bets to the gamblers and there's no really accurate price signal coming out of that. So does that serve such an important function? Probably not. And it's fair to say the same about prediction markets on sports. Does anyone really need to know the outcome of a sports game that badly? I mean, probably not. I don't have anything against it per se, because people spend money for entertainment on other things. I mean, this is another way to spend your money. But it's not as valuable as prediction markets in some other categories. Right?

I mean, I think I've just always had a motivation to learn more about what I'm interested in. So when I start learning about something, I just get it all in my head and then I can talk about it pretty competently, I guess. I wouldn't consider myself to have natural interviewing skill. I just think I know a lot about the things that I'm interested in.

So for news, mostly Bloomberg. For social media, mostly Twitter. And then I also read articles on Substack.

So I think I had written about Sam on Twitter a little bit, and it got picked up by the person who was at the time running Sam's Twitter account. And they said, "I run this Twitter account now, but I think you have some smart ideas about Sam. Would you be interested in taking over the Twitter account?" And I was like, "Oh, yeah, that could be fun." And my dad was like, "No, you can't do that. I don't want to get sued or anything." So we ended up talking to Sam's parents about it, and they were disappointed that I wouldn't be able to take over the Twitter account. But as an alternative, they proposed, "You should just interview Sam for your podcast." So I just thought, "Wow, that's a great idea. Let's do that."

Oh, I don't know. I think they were impressed with my knowledge of various parts of his criminal case, which we actually didn't cover very much during our podcast together, since it's already been widely covered. But, yeah, I think I just had learned a lot about the case and they were like, "Well, maybe we want someone who knows a lot about the case to be able to take over his Twitter."

I don't know. I might want to skip that one for legal reasons.

I mean, I've watched so many of his other interviews, both when he was behind bars and before that, and I feel like he talks the same way to everyone. So I'm 14, you would expect maybe the average person is going to talk a little bit differently to a 14-year-old interviewer. But for him, I think it was pretty much the same, which is kind of what I expected. He's very consistent when he's talking to different people.

So when he picked up and was like, "Hi, it's Sam," I was like, "Wow, I've heard him say this in so many other interviews, but he's talking to me. That's crazy." He also called 15 minutes before the scheduled time, so I was panicking a little bit trying to get all my questions in order and deciding what order I was going to ask them in. I mean, it was pretty intense. And also, it was split up over two days in three hour windows during each day, since he can only call for 15 minutes at a time. So that was a little bit stressful.

I mean, it's mostly what I expected. He just hadn't really gone on the record about it specifically, which is why I wanted to ask him. I think his views are pretty common. He's a part of the effective altruism community. So I wasn't so surprised when he said he thought there was a 25% chance of AI destroying humanity. Obviously, if it's the average person, that might seem a little surprising. But knowing him, I wasn't very surprised.

I think there's going to be a lot of benefit in the short term, especially when we're seeing the rate of technological progress. Just in the past few months, AI has solved multiple millennium problems, which has been a huge deal. So I think there's definitely potential of AI curing diseases over the short term. But in the long term, you have to consider that there's a few examples of less intelligent things controlling more intelligent things, and that's kind of the whole point that the doomers are trying to make. Just that, when humans were smarter than the next smartest animal, we’re the ones who dominated, right?

At the end of the interview, I asked him what I call the coin flip question. "Would you take a 51-49 bet of doubling the world or destroying it?" And I asked him, "Would you take a 51-49 bet of being free tomorrow or doubling your prison time?" So I mean, there's a couple other interesting questions there I would've loved to get his take on.

Yeah. I mean, there's something funny that happened. Someone at my school walked up to me and they were like, "Hey, are you the kid who ..." Actually, wait. I actually don't want to go there.

But they were all excited. They thought it was pretty funny, and then they were impressed that it got as many views as it did. I think right now it's at about 1.3 million views, probably closer to 1.4 across all platforms. But, yeah, I think everyone was very surprised that it was able to do that well. And mostly people just think it's funny. Some responses that have been less good were people focusing on the ad read I did during the episode and mistaking it for a sportsbook, even though it's actually a free-to-play forecasting competition. So that's been the less good side of things.

Ninth grade. And I live in Westchester County, New York.

It's a good question. Maybe Marc Andreessen, in the short term.

Yeah. I'm involved a little bit with the new media team at his company, and so that would be pretty cool.

#6605. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6604. Vogue’s Best Dressed List of 2026 Is Live! Here’s How to Recreate Our Favorite Looks of the Year

From the red-carpet heavy-hitters to Hollywood’s next generation of stars and the stylists making it all happen, the honorees on our 2026 best-dressed list all share a love for a great outfit. It certainly helps that we do too—which is why we’re coming in with the cold, hard facts: We’re breaking down their style signifiers, one shoppable piece at a time.

The names on this year’s list range from celebrity street style regulars—see: Jennifer Lawrence—to relative newcomers like actor Sarah Pidgeon and singer Gracie Abrams. Model and CFDA judge Paloma Elsesser and actor Ayo Edebiri both appear for their second year in a row on Vogue’s Best Dressed list.

Ahead, you’ll have the chance to browse through some of the honorees’ best looks of 2026, with a snapshot of the key pieces that made those outfits stand out to us—and in turn, dominate the sartorial conversation at Vogue HQ. Some stars championed CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund nominees early on: Edebiri and Lee both wore Lii for press appearances this year, while Lawrence sported one of Colleen Allen’s velvet house coats with a white tee and slippers on a mild fall day in New York. Others are vintage fiends at heart—Elsesser, who self-styled her Vogue Shopping cover shoot in September—chief among them; her everyday looks comprise a mix of vintage Junya Watanabe and Comme des Garçons and emerging designers.

Below, a snapshot of the wardrobes that make up Vogue’s Best Dressed list of 2026, complete with the key pieces needed to shop their signature looks and make them your own.

A regular fixture in our weekly celeb outfits roundups, Jennifer Lawrence is known for her effortless brand of messy-chic, cool-mom-at-drop-off looks, often centered around a ball cap and a slubby vintage tee. The Row and Khaite are mainstay labels in rotation, though, let the record show that she loves mixing more eclectic pieces—like her Colleen Allen velvet house coat—with simple basics (Leset is noted a go-to).

Sarah Pidgeon’s debut on Vogue’s Best Dressed List comes as no surprise: Since playing the role of ’90s style icon, Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy on Ryan Murphy’s Love Story, Pidgeon has taken method acting to a new level with method dressing. For the majority of her public appearances, Pidgeon has stepped out in pieces reflective of Bessette-Kennedy’s refrained style, like a Yohji Yamamoto dress, a collarless Aflalo leather trench, and an embellished mint green slip from Chanel.

Model and CFDA judge Paloma Elsesser is a modern cool-girl, known for her IYKYK approach to dressing . A champion of emerging designers like the London-based, Central Saint Martins graduate Goyagoma, her eclectic style is typically supplemented by vintage grails from the likes Junya Watanabe and Comme des Garçons. For those who worship at the altar of “quiet luxury,” Elsesser eschews that with bold prints, vivid color, and a style that’s all her own.

Like her repertoire of acting roles (TV: The Bear, film: Clarissa, Broadway: Proof), Ayo Edebiri’s style shows as much range as her career choices—from repping emerging designers like Giovanna Flores in a patchwork dress to Conner Ives in pinstripe suiting (yes, the same Ives whose fur-trimmed coat just broke the internet), to her more mature choices for the red carpet, such as Chanel and The Row. Edebiri doesn’t limit herself to one style or silhouette—she can go from feminine dressing to masculine suiting, just as easily as she can shift into various characters (Pacino, anyone?).

Known for her starring roles in this year’s Toy Story 5, as well as in Tron: Ares, and Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, actor Greta Lee’s sartorial choices take a page out of her action-flick lineup, albeit, with a fashion-forward twist. A fan of bold color-blocking, Lee has worn CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund winner Lii, as well as a fire-engine red fringed gown by High Sport to the London premiere of Toy Story 5, while making bold fashion choices with Marc Jacobs’s iconic blue sequin strapless top from the spring 2026 collection.

It’s been a banner year for the actress Carey Mulligan—in March, she accepted a royal honor in the form of a CBE (Commander of the Order of the British Empire) from King Charles III for her services to drama. Even at Windsor Castle, she used the opportunity to show up in a royally-fashionable ensemble (one, we might say, was fit for a king!) wearing a jacket and trousers from The Row, accessorized with Jacques Marie Mage sunglasses. Then, for the season two premiere of Beef in which she plays a starring role, Mulligan showed up in a pixelated floral skirt and brocade bustier top from designer Julian Klausner’s fall 2026 collection for Dries Van Noten. Her red carpet looks are a mix of sumptuous color, pattern, and texture, illustrated best in a full Colleen Allen look composed of a ruffled velvet top with a coordinating silk column skirt in sunburnt orange.

Another one in Lii’s fashionable girl-gang, actor Whitney Peak (who stars as Lenore Dove Baird in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping) appreciates a color-blocked ensemble, whether it’s for a magazine launch or a press appearance (the latter saw her in London-based designer Torishéju). Her color palettes skews minimalist—think neutrals punctuated by flashes of red—but the silhouettes she gravitates towards are anything but. Case in point: the knitted black Diotima dress she wore to the Academy Museum Gala in Los Angeles was a maximalist’s dream.

Actor Tessa Thompson has been delivering on the red carpet for years now — and her style only continues to bring the wow-factor, from being a fellow fan of Giovanna Flores’s patchwork dress to Kallmeyer’s tailored suiting. She’s known to love a sharp, structured shoulder, and has a penchant for contrasting a delicate silk dress with a strong leather jacket paired. With her Golden Globes nomination for Hedda, starring in the Netflix thriller His & Hers, and a Broadway debut in Fear of 13, co-starring Adrien Brody, Thompson’s style is one that delivers as much variety and star power as her resume.

Our mother in style, Tracee Ellis Ross’s wardrobe is as bright as her star power. With this year’s Broadway debut in Every Brilliant Thing and a daytime Emmy for her show, Solo Traveling, she stepped up her style game even further, with the help of her stylist Law Roach. The Girlfriends and Black-ish star has been experimenting with color and texture as of late, stepping out in highly-saturated ensembles that span an embellished Prada skirt and button-down (look 22 from the fall runway), a marigold tasseled gown by Balenciaga (designed by Pierpaolo Piccioli for spring 2027), and punchy Dries Van Noten (look 35, also from SS27).

After returning to the stage this year with a 16-show sold out residency at Paris’s Plénitude Arena, Celine Dion delivered what the people wanted—and so much more. With daily paparazzi shots that showed off her good humor in style, she stepped out in looks that ranged from suede Jacquemus to all-black leather Tom Ford. Quintessential French design, in feather-trimmed Dior and custom Chanel (she wore a gown that was recreation of her 1997 Oscars dress) rounded out this Canadian in Paris’s sojourn.

The former First Lady has been having fun with fashion as of late—donning a Thom Browne suit set for a ribbon-cutting at the Barack Obama Presidential Center one day to a custom Acne Studios skirt printed with a photo of her late mother, Marian Robinson, the next. At the US Open this summer, she wore a red, white, and navy blue striped Chanel dress from the resort 2027 collection.

Ever since the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards, we haven’t been able to get Gracie Abrams as a gothic vision in Colleen Allen out of our minds. The singer has been serving looks long before that though, stepping out in her signature mix of vintage tees, Conner Ives rugby polos and trousers, and an enviable collection of Chanel pumps. Equal parts comfy and stylish, she’s known to wear a quirky mashup of styles and designers.

#6603. The Ralph Lauren Black Friday Sale Is My Own Private Polofest

#6602. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

#6601. 11 Leftover Turkey Sandwiches to Look Forward To

It is a universal truth that the food the day after Thanksgiving is just as exciting (if not more so) as what’s served on the holiday itself. With a fridge full of Thanksgiving leftovers, the possibilities are endless. But leftovers reach their most perfect form in a sandwich, where all the components play off one other for a few transcendent bites.

These Thanksgiving sandwiches make the most of what you’ve got, whether that’s a few slices of turkey or enough stuffing and cranberry sauce for an encore. Go all in with a gooey melt, load a pita with spiced turkey and crunchy vegetables, or give turkey the chicken salad treatment. There’s no need for post-holiday blues when a leftover turkey sandwich is on the horizon.

This turkey sandwich takes inspiration from one of the all-time greats: the tuna melt. You might be surprised by how well turkey takes to the format. For the full diner experience, serve it with potato chips and a dill pickle.

These leftover turkey sliders have a lot going on, in the best way. Picture: melty cheese, cranberry mayo, garlic butter, turkey, mashed potatoes, and more where that came from.

Give your Thanksgiving leftovers the club treatment by layering turkey and cranberry sauce with crisp bacon and lettuce. And don’t forget that middle slide of bread. We’re not animals, after all.

Need a break from heavy Thanksgiving fare but still have turkey to use up? Shred it, toss it with butter-bloomed spices, and tuck it into a pita with a bright, tangy slaw.

In this play on a turkey club, the middle slice of bread gets swapped out for leftover stuffing fried in bacon fat. (We repeat: stuffing fried in bacon fat.)

Turkey and cranberry sauce already have a salty-sweet thing going on. Why not play that up by swapping plain bread for custardy French toast?

Sometimes it’s best to keep a leftover turkey sandwich simple. Turkey, cranberry sauce, cheese, and fresh sage, pressed until golden, give you all the flavors of Thanksgiving in four ingredients (plus bread).

Though the recipe calls for cooked chicken, you guessed it—you can swap in leftover turkey seamlessly. The apple and fennel both provide lots of crunch and freshness.

Another chicken banger that works beautifully with leftover turkey. Boosted with red curry paste, tangy from Greek yogurt, this mixture is as good stuffed into lettuce cups as it is tucked between sliced bread.

This recipe sticks close to the classic turkey club, with one simple twist: a punchy, verdant herb mayo that comes together in seconds in the blender.

Roast turkey, tangy sauerkraut, melty Swiss cheese, and a tangy sauce? Heaven. Bonus points if the rye bread you use is studded with caraway seeds.
